stories.headline: Hyderabad’s Ganesh puja: Big on devotion, bigger on moolah
stories.deck: From flower showers and sound systems to giant cranes and record-breaking laddu auctions, Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in Hyderabad sets money flowing across a vast network of businesses, workers and public agencies. The trail runs from the costs borne by organisers to the contracts, livelihoods and public expenditure that sustain the 10-day festival, from the first preparations to the final…
stories.bodyText:
A helicopter hovering over a Ganesh idol is not an everyday sight, even in a city that goes all out for its biggest festival. On September 24, as an immersion procession wound its way towards the Hussainsagar, the six-seater Airbus H125 showered the idol with flower petals from above. It was a fleeting spectacle, but one that involved considerable logistical arrangements and expense. And it was only a small part of the elaborate machinery that keeps Hyderabad’s Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations running.
Behind the towering idols, elaborate pandals and processions that stretch late into the night lies an economy of its own. Idol-makers, decorators, sound operators, transporters, crane companies, caterers and scores of workers find business in the festival while organisers marshal donations and sponsorships to pay for the spectacle.
The flower shower was organised by Hanuman Youth Association, which installed an idol in Bowrampet.
“An aviation agent contacted me for parking space for the helicopter. It was to arrive from Bengaluru, shower petals on the second day and leave on the third. Since the Rajiv Gandhi International Airport and Begumpet Airport charge a lot, they looked at my aerofarm as a parking spot,” says P.R. Singh, owner of Singh Aerofarm in Sangareddy and a retired Indian Air Force squadron leader.
Mr. Singh estimates that the operation, including the related arrangements, could have cost the organisers around ₹20 lakh.
Crunching the numbers
There is no single account book for Ganesh Chaturthi in Hyderabad. The Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi (BGUS) estimates that the festival generates ₹6,000 crore to ₹7,000 crore in economic activity in the city.
BGUS general secretary R. Shashidhar says the festival provides direct employment to around two lakh families and indirect employment to another 4.5 lakh people. Other estimates put the economic activity at upwards of ₹10,000 crore when months of preparation are factored in.
The money flows from organisers to idol-makers, tent-house operators, decorators, lighting contractors, transporters, sound-system providers, bands, flower sellers, caterers and other workers. Expenditure ranges from a few thousand rupees to several lakhs, beginning well before the idol reaches the mandap.
According to Telangana Police, around 1.24 lakh Ganesh idols were registered on the State’s Ganesh portal this year. This figure covers all of Telangana, not just Hyderabad. Director General of Police C.V. Anand says the actual number across the State could range from 3.5 lakh to 4 lakh if idols installed in homes, apartments and other private premises were included.
Expenditure varies with the scale of the celebrations. A small neighbourhood mandap may spend relatively little on the idol, structure and decoration, while a large one can incur costs running into several lakhs on the pandal, lighting, flowers, manpower and other arrangements.
At Balapur, one of Hyderabad’s best-known Ganesh celebrations, the committee spent around ₹98 lakh on the festival last year, says Kalyan Niranjan Reddy, chairman of the Balapur Ganesh Utsava Samithi. The amount covered the idol, workers, flowers, decoration and pandal arrangements. The committee is yet to complete its accounts for this year.
Mr. Reddy says around ₹30 lakh to ₹40 lakh was collected through chanda (contributions). The remainder came from other donations, advertisements and sponsorships. The procession adds to these expenses, creating another stream of business for transporters, sound operators and other service providers.
At Balapur, the 21-foot idol required a heavy vehicle, says Kalyan Reddy. The vehicle, driver and diesel together cost around ₹40,000.
The expense generates business for transporters, vehicle owners, drivers and workers involved in loading and securing the idol. At major immersion points, cranes and other equipment are also needed to lower idols into the water.
The next bill is often heard before it is seen. For a small mandap, a basic speaker arrangement can cost around ₹5,000 to ₹6,000, while a DJ setup can cost around ₹15,000 for eight hours, says Hyderabad-based sound-system operator Mohammed Saber Hussain.
“Usually, DJs and sound operators have an eight-hour booking period because that is considered the industry standard,” he explains. The actual amount depends on the size of the system, the equipment hired and the duration.
Larger packages combining sound boxes, truss structures, lighting and DJ equipment can cost up to ₹75,000. Hussain says he also received a booking worth ₹2 lakh during this year’s festival season. Packages vary according to the equipment hired, while the customer bears generator and diesel costs.
Traditional performers also find business during the festival. Marfa bands charged around ₹20,000 to ₹40,000 for performances this year, with popular troupes commanding ₹50,000 to ₹60,000 on immersion day.
Unlike many Hyderabad processions, the Balapur Ganesh Utsava Samithi does not hire DJs. It has followed the tradition of playing bhajans on immersion day since the 1980s. Yet its total festival expenditure was around ₹98 lakh last year, reflecting the cumulative cost of the many arrangements that go into the celebrations.
Prasadam adds another layer of spending, covering ingredients, cooking, packaging, transport and distribution, says Shashidhar. At a large mandap, food distributed to thousands of devotees over several days can add up to a substantial bill, even when the per-person cost is modest.
Beyond the obvious
The expenditure extends beyond the organisers to the government, which provides electricity and deploys personnel and equipment for immersion arrangements.
This year, the Telangana Southern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGSPDCL) supplied free electricity to 51,207 registered Ganesh idols and pandals across its 21 circles, with a sanctioned connected load of 1.12 lakh kW.
The government’s estimated expenditure this year was ₹17.8 crore, up from ₹15.59 crore in 2025-26, when 47,649 pandals received free power.
Public spending also covers the personnel and infrastructure needed to manage the celebrations. Power utility staff worked round the clock to monitor feeders, transformers, lighting and emergency arrangements, particularly at major immersion points.
Anand says more than 25,000 police personnel were deployed in Hyderabad for immersion arrangements over the 10-day festival period. Cranes, barricades, traffic management, sanitation, lighting, emergency services and waste removal add to the logistical costs.
The scale of the immersion operation is evident in the cranes deployed along major routes.
Syed Faraz and Syed Ausaf, owners of Super Cranes, which participates in the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation’s (GHMC) immersion operations, says 10 cranes were deployed at NTR Marg and 12 at People’s Plaza. Their capacities varied according to the size and weight of the idols.
GHMC norms require cranes with a minimum capacity of 50 tonnes, they point out. “The Khairatabad Ganesh idol required a much larger machine for immersion: a SANY SAC 3000 crane with a capacity of 300 to 350 tonnes, an 80-metre main boom and 100 tonnes of counterweights,” says Faraz.
Transporting the crane requires at least three 40-foot trailers, accompanied by a signal-flag vehicle to guide the convoy through narrow roads and sharp turns. The six-axle crane has 12 tyres and may require traffic management even before reaching the immersion site, the owners say. “Moving such a machine to an immersion site is itself a logistical operation.”
Each crane requires five skilled workers and a skilled rigger for safe lifting operations, with one supervisor deployed for every five cranes. Workers are provided orange jerseys and identity cards at the immersion sites.
Unlike private bookings by Ganesh committees, the immersion crane operations are awarded through the GHMC tender process. The contract runs for 12 days, with 12-hour shifts during the first eight days and 24-hour shifts thereafter.
Operators inspect sites six to seven days before deployment, assessing the idol’s weight and height, lifting radius and other conditions to determine the required crane capacity and commercial terms.
Super Cranes executed the GHMC work in association with other crane operators deployed at various immersion points.
Laddu auction and local causes
If the festival has an economy of expenditure, it also has an economy of transactions that can be difficult to explain in ordinary terms.
Balapur’s famous 21-kg Ganesh laddu fetched a record ₹39 lakh at auction this year. Sama Praneeth Reddy of Urban Realty Group won the bid, surpassing last year’s ₹35 lakh. Nine participants had registered for the auction, including representatives of five companies, while one bidder participated from London.
At Keerthi Richmond Villas in Bandlaguda Jagir, a 5-kg Ganesh laddu fetched ₹1.01 crore this year, compared with ₹2.31 crore last year. Despite weighing a quarter as much as Balapur’s laddu, it fetched more than twice the latter’s auction price. Such bids illustrate how the value attached to the laddu can far exceed its production cost.
In both cases, the auction proceeds are separate from festival expenditure and generally go towards community development, welfare or other local causes.
There is no price tag on the festival itself. But almost every part of putting it together — from installing an idol to lowering it into the lake — comes at a cost. Together, these expenses, along with the businesses, jobs and transactions the festival generates, form an economy that runs alongside the celebrations.

stories.headline: Marginalised Yanadi and Chenchu communities in Andhra Pradesh struggle for land
stories.deck: Caught in a cycle of landlessness, insecure housing, precarious livelihoods, and neglect, the Yanadi and Chenchu settlements in Andhra Pradesh remain highly marginalised. Despite government welfare schemes, a stark gap persists between their living conditions and surrounding urban areas
stories.bodyText:
On one side lies the bustle of Poranki Centre in Vijayawada city, where gridlocked traffic, thriving shops, and a sprawling residential colony dictate the rhythms of everyday life. On the other, about 40 Yanadi families are living in a world completely detached from urban civilisation. Though separated by barely a few kilometres, the true distance between these two worlds is measured in their access to education, healthcare, secure livelihoods, and basic amenities.
Poranki, a prominent neighbourhood within the Penamaluru mandal of the Vijayawada revenue division, contains pockets where contrasting realities exist side by side. In Prabhu Nagar, a spacious residential area reached by a narrow lane branching off the main thoroughfare, the contrast becomes stark just beyond a pre-primary Anganwadi centre.
Here, a pathway covered in mud and slush gives way to a cramped, filthy alley of makeshift shelters. Pieced together from frayed plastic sheets and tarpaulins, these dwellings lack even basic doors or windows. A short walk through this landscape reveals children running barefoot through the muck, and women sitting on iron cots outside their shelters—some quietly combing their hair, others talking in hushed tones. There is little movement here, and even less cheer. It is a settlement suspended in a state of deprivation, despite being within easy reach of the mainstream world.
The true depth of the families’ predicament becomes clear within minutes. Their makeshift shelters sit precariously on a small portion of private land that doubles as a Christian burial ground. A few graves lie startlingly close to the dwellings. Pointing toward one of the weathered mounds, Thupakula Pottamma, a woman in her fifties, quietly says it is where her mother-in-law was buried a few years ago. “We live where the dead rest. We too will join them when we die,” she says, her voice choking.
Making matters worse, the landowners have repeatedly asked the families to vacate the property. Yet, the residents insist they have nowhere else to go. Over the years, they have knocked on the doors of local officials and ruling party leaders, pleading for a piece of land where they can finally relocate and build secure lives.
“Years have passed, but no alternative has materialised,” says Subbamma. “The one time we pressed for a solution, the authorities said they would shift us to either Onkuru or Pulipaka. But it seemed like they were only saying that to ward us off,” she adds.
Slushy pathways
And their problems don’t end there. When it rains, the settlement is quickly inundated, forcing the families to take shelter in the Anganwadi building or in the cellar of a nearby apartment complex, an arrangement facilitated by a local TDP leader.
“The pathway to our homes becomes so slushy that we can hardly walk on it. After repeated requests, the local authorities laid gravel on it, but the recent heavy rains washed it all away. There is no sign of the gravel now,” says Durga Bhavani, pointing to the muddy, slush-filled pathway.
Another problem is that no one in the community, young or old, seems to know their age. “I don’t know. It is mentioned on my Aadhaar card, which I got only recently,” says Eega Eeswar, who looks barely old enough to be the father of three children.
For a living, the men go fishing in the nearby canals or scavenging for recyclable waste, while some of the women venture out to collect waste to supplement the meagre household income. Even before the break of dawn, they go out, rummaging around for plastic, tins, metal pieces, and other discarded material to make anywhere between ₹200 and ₹300 by selling them to the local scrap dealer.
For children in the settlement, the divide begins early, making education a distant dream. However, intervention by a local NGO has helped a few children enrol in the nearby Zilla Parishad school, offering them a chance to break out of the cycle of deprivation.
“It took us a long time to persuade the families to send their children to school. They take time to trust outsiders,” says Vasantha Kumari from Navajeevan Bala Bhavan (NJBB), an NGO working for the rescue and rehabilitation of children and youth from troubled backgrounds.
For Lakshmi, that trust has transformed into a sense of pride. Watching her 11-year-old daughter, Charmudi, return home in a school uniform alongside a few other children, her face lights up. “She is very talented,” Lakshmi says softly. “She even won first prize in a drawing competition.”
In a settlement otherwise defined by deprivation, Charmudi’s success, and her mother’s quiet pride, stand as living proof of what can be achieved if only the children here are given an equal opportunity.
The lack of access is also evident inside these dark, dingy dwellings, which contain little beyond the bare essentials—such as iron cots, a few cooking utensils, and, in some dwellings, old wooden tables piled with used clothes and other belongings. Each shelter has a bulb, but electricity is available only from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. A couple of solar lights donated by the NGO in the common area provide some relief, allowing the children to sit outside and do their homework after dusk.
Life continues
The picture is much the same across the plains of Andhra Pradesh, with several Yanadi settlements caught between insecure housing, precarious livelihoods, and poor access to basic amenities, even when they are located within or close to expanding urban and semi-urban settlements.
“The Yanadis are a historically mobile community, with Reddy Yanadis generally better off and Challa Yanadis among the more impoverished sections. Their problems are particularly acute in the plains, where many continue to live on the margins of society,” says Alladi Deva Kumar, founder and executive secretary of Dalit Bahujan Resource Centre that works to empower marginalised communities.
One of the most serious concerns, he says, is the lack of institutional deliveries among Yanadi women. “With many children born outside formal healthcare facilities, securing birth certificates and Aadhaar cards becomes difficult. The absence of identity documents, in turn, can prevent children from enrolling in schools and accessing various government welfare schemes,” says Deva Kumar.
Citing another example of about 250 ST (Yanadi) families living in Kala Chakra Colony in Amaravati mandal of Guntur district, who have been struggling without basic amenities for nearly two decades, he says the colony lacks drinking water, sanitation, and toilets, while 37 children have no Anganwadi facility and 55 students have to travel 3 km to attend school. As many as 130 families continue to live in makeshift tents.
If the Yanadi experience illustrates the vulnerability of a historically mobile community in the plains, the experience of the Chenchus points to another dimension of tribal displacement: the movement of a forest-dependent Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG) community toward the fringes of towns and cities.
Although Chenchus’ vulnerability is officially recognised through their classification as a PVTG community, many of them, after being pushed out of their habitats in forests, have moved to the fringes of towns and cities, where the loss of traditional livelihoods has not necessarily translated into better access to housing, education, healthcare, and other services.
A stark manifestation of this crisis unfolded nearly a decade ago at B.B.R. Nagar in Kankipadu, Krishna district. Today, a row of makeshift shelters lines the main thoroughfare—a settlement that surfaced after about 20 Chenchu families were driven out of a nearby locality by residents who demanded their removal from the area. “The good thing about this place is that it is beside the canal, where our men can catch fish. But living here has its own challenges. We have put up temporary shelters, but rainwater drips through the roof during the monsoon, and snakes and other creatures also get inside because there is no proper flooring,” says Avala Sivamma, a mother of three. Sivamma, who works as a domestic helper in a few households in the nearby localities, does her best to keep the family going and put food on the table, as whatever little her husband earns through fishing is spent on alcohol.
Despite their living challenges, the 20 households have managed to obtain a public tap for water supply. Earlier, their children, who went to school without taking a bath for want of water, were sent back by teachers who asked them to bathe and come. Housing is another major concern. “Grant of pattas for the land we occupy will solve our major problem,” says Mariyamma, a mother of three.
For activists working with these communities, however, the problem goes beyond the immediate deficits in housing, land, and basic services. It also raises questions about political representation and the ability of fragmented communities to articulate a common demand.
“Along with the Denotified Tribes (DNTs), the communities that were historically brought under the colonial Criminal Tribes Acts and subsequently denotified after Independence, it is true that Scheduled Tribes like Yanadis and Chenchus have also faced severe socio-economic vulnerability,” says M. Subba Rao, an activist fighting for DNT rights for the last three decades.
Political representation of the communities, he says, is the only way out. “Lack of political maturity has kept fragmented social and political groups belonging to these communities from uniting for a common cause,” he says ruefully, alleging that some activists seek proximity to upper-caste power centres, which exploit divisions among DNT communities and leaders to retain their influence.
On paper and reality
The scale of the challenge is reflected in the State’s own data on its most vulnerable tribal communities. Andhra Pradesh has a total population of 4,95,77,700, of which the ST population is 27,39,504 (5.53%). According to the 2023 PVTG survey, the State had a PVTG population of 4,88,329, comprising 1,28,663 PVTG households belonging to 11 communities, including Chenchu, Bodo Gadaba, Guto Gadaba, Kondareddi, Dongria Khond, Kutia Khond, Bondo Porja, Khond Porja, Parangi Porja, Konda Savaras, and Kolam.
Several government initiatives have sought to address these shortcomings. The State Tribal Welfare Department officials say efforts are being made to improve the socio-economic status of PVTGs by bridging gaps in health, education, and livelihoods, and by saturating PVTG communities and families with basic facilities and services under the Central scheme PM-JANMAN (Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan).
According to officials, the scheme is being implemented through 11 interventions, including housing, roads, drinking water, healthcare, education, electrification, mobile connectivity, and livelihood support. Under the housing component, 43,593 houses have been sanctioned against 50,636 identified gaps, with 11,074 completed. For road connectivity, 303 works covering 866 km have been sanctioned to connect 341 habitations, of which 132 km has been completed.
The officials claim that under piped water supply, 99,865 of 1.80 lakh PVTG households have been provided tap connections, achieving 55.54% coverage, with works sanctioned for another 500 habitations. Healthcare is being provided through 156 Mobile Medical Units covering all the PVTG habitations. “The Government is also trying to reach out to the ST population through Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DA-JGUA),” said the department’s Additional Director M. Saraswathi.
Despite the existence of schemes aimed at uplifting ST, PVTG and DNT communities, many continue to face issues involving landlessness, casual labour, insecure housing, education, documentation, access to welfare and integration into society.
Scattered settlements along canals and tank bunds and on the fringes of villages and towns may be located close to mainstream residential areas, but they face severe isolation. The question is not merely whether government schemes reach tribal communities, but whether the schemes are designed around the way those communities actually live.

stories.headline: Oil prices soar to $103 per barrel again as Middle East supply concerns intensify
stories.deck: Recent developments have led to a surge in oil prices, largely driven by new restrictions placed on Chinese fuel exports. This, combined with reports of increased US military presence in the Middle East, has heightened concerns over supply stability. Following the escalation of conflict between the US and Israel regarding Iran, both Brent and WTI crude prices have risen sharply.
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices edged higher on Friday as fresh restrictions on Chinese fuel exports and reports of increased US military deployments to the Middle East kept supply concerns in focus.
Brent crude stood at $102.60, higher by 28 cents or 0.27% while WTI crude was trading at $92.96, up 9 cents or 0.10%.
The moves came after a sharp rally in the previous session. Brent gained more than $4 on Thursday, while WTI rose by over $2 after reports that the US was sending additional troops and aircraft carriers to the Middle East. News that China had halted fuel exports further heightened concerns about a potential worsening of global fuel shortages.
Despite the recent rise, Brent remained on course for a 1.93% weekly decline. The benchmark had gained 14% overall in September, while WTI posted a more modest 4% rise last month.
According to the Wall Street Journal, US was sending a third aircraft carrier and as many as 10,000 additional troops to the Middle East. The move came as President Donald Trump weighed whether to resume strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.
"Now I have to make a decision. They'll either sign a very fair deal, or they won't exist any longer," Trump told reporters at the White House.
China's decision on fuel exports was another source of concern for oil markets. Beijing had restricted fuel exports in March following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, before easing those curbs in July. It has since been managing shipments of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel on a monthly basis.
China began a weeklong holiday on Thursday, with major refiners not receiving approval to export to regions outside Hong Kong and Macau in October, according to sources. It was not immediately clear whether Beijing would again permit refiners to export fuel once the holiday ends on October 7.
Meanwhile, the US administration has asked Germany and France to reduce emergency diesel inventories in an effort to ease soaring global fuel prices, according to three people.
As the Middle East conflict has stretched beyond seven months, oil markets have remained volatile, although prices have been relatively calmer than the sharp spike to $126 a barrel seen earlier.

stories.headline: 'He has good ideas': Putin lauds PM Modi's peace push to end Russia-Ukraine war
stories.bodyText:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday lauded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to seek an end to the Ukraine conflict, saying that he has “good ideas” for achieving a peaceful resolution.
"Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good and even friendly relations, personal good relations, constantly raises the question and asks the question about putting an end to the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.
Asked about the issue at the Valdai Club forum, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been actively working to find mutually acceptable solutions to the Ukraine conflict.
"He has an avid interest and very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. In that sense, naturally, the Prime Minister takes a neutral position but with an interest in the end of the conflict. I think it's my duty to say that directly. And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas," Putin said.
Putin thanked PM Modi for his efforts and continued support for resolving the Ukraine conflict through dialogue.
"We are thankful for his desire to put an end to this conflict through peaceful means and as soon as possible," he added.
Prime Minister Modi and Putin last met in September on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where they discussed strengthening trade ties, including the implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, along with cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence and culture.
PM Modi has repeatedly called for peace, stressing that India has maintained a principled and humanitarian approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
"India has maintained a principled and humanitarian stance on the conflict which is equally appreciated by both President Putin and President Zelenskyy. In line with this, both the leaders spoke to me to share their perspectives on the developments related to the conflict. I reiterated India's principled and consistent stand and encouraged dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict," the Prime Minister said during an interview with Japanese news outlet 'The Yomiuri Shimbun' while on a visit to the country in August.
Responding to a question on India’s role in peace efforts between the two countries, Prime Minister Modi said, "I have already indicated India's willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict. I believe, by virtue of our good relations with both sides, including key stakeholders, we can strengthen efforts dedicated to the restoration of an early and lasting peace in Ukraine."
This comes as Putin reiterated Moscow’s long-standing position that Russia has no plans to attack European countries, while warning that it would respond to any aggression with “all weapons” at its disposal.
He also accused Western countries, particularly in Europe, of escalating tensions by discussing preparations for a possible war with Moscow, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea and seizing Russian vessels.
European leaders and intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could be capable of launching an attack on another country within the next few years, particularly if it emerges victorious from the war in Ukraine.

briefs.headline: Bumpy Ride: Private bus sector in Keralam staring at a crisis
briefs.deck: While the Priyadarshini free travel scheme has brought cheers to women passengers in Keralam, it has dealt a body blow to the private bus sector, which has already been struggling from dwindling revenues and high operational costs
briefs.bodyText:
It was raining intermittently on a cloudy evening when a private bus on the Attingal–Venjaramoodu route entered the crowded Attingal private bus stand in Thiruvananthapuram in Keralam.
Even before the engine fell silent, the bus crew spotted another bus at the stand—a service that, according to the route schedule, should have left the stand around 30 seconds ago. Within moments, a heated argument began between the crew of the two buses. The crew of the former bus alleged that the latter bus was eating into their business by deliberately delaying its departure and poaching passengers. After several minutes of heated exchanges, the latter bus finally left the stand, with only a handful of passengers.
Though that confrontation ended there, another, milder altercation erupted inside the former bus. The owner-turned-conductor directed his frustration towards the driver. Throughout the journey, the conductor had repeatedly urged the driver to speed through the heavy evening traffic, skip some stops and ensure that the bus reached the stand on schedule.
K.N. Rajesh (name changed), a middle-aged driver with around 22 years of experience at the wheel, said no amount of skill acquired over the years could have helped him beat the heavy evening traffic in the town and the delay was unavoidable. Yet, the bus had lost a handful of passengers as it arrived about 30 seconds late. The delay will cause a cascading effect on passenger numbers at nearly half the stops along the route, he says.
“As bus workers, we try to avoid such situations. In our bid to maintain time and minimise losses, we may inadvertently commit minor traffic violations such as jumping a red signal at the last moment or skipping certain stops or services,” says Rajesh.
The episode offers a glimpse into the daily dramas unfolding across Keralam’s public transport network, where intense competition, fuelled by dwindling revenues of private bus operators, has become commonplace. The situation has worsened since the State government introduced the Priyadarshini free travel scheme on Ordinary buses of the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) for women and transgender persons on June 15, 2026.
Janatha Sabu, a private bus owner and member of the Kerala Motor Transport Workers’ Welfare Fund Board, notes that the industry has been in the doldrums since the COVID-19 outbreak, with nearly a third of its passenger base switching to alternative modes of transport. The Priyadarshini scheme has now dealt another severe blow to the already struggling private bus industry, eroding more than 50% of its existing passenger base, observes Sabu.
The resulting scramble for getting passengers has intensified competition and turned bus stands across the State into venues of frequent confrontations. The scheme, a poll promise of the United Democratic Front, has now emerged as a major success, with women passengers embracing the scheme. Transport Minister C.P. John says the scheme had facilitated an average 12.93 lakh free journeys a day in 100 days, entailing a financial liability of around ₹267 crore for the KSRTC.
While acknowledging the scheme’s popularity, the private bus operators say they are not entirely opposed to it, even though it had severely affected their livelihood.
700 private buses stop operations
T. Gopinathan, general secretary of the All Kerala Bus Operators Organisation, says that around 700 private buses had ceased operations during the first 100 days of the scheme. More than half of the buses still in operation are reportedly running reduced services and earning low daily revenues.
“The State government should hike the minimum fare to ₹15 for all categories of passengers, along with an increase in student fares, to offset the losses suffered by private buses. Otherwise, the private bus sector will face a slow death,” says Gopinathan.
Daily revenue has fallen by around ₹2,000 to ₹3,000 for private buses operating in southern Keralam, where KSRTC services are more extensive than in the central and northern parts of the State.
Many operators are left with barely ₹500 to ₹1,000 in daily profit after meeting fuel expenses, employees’ wages and maintenance costs. Fuel prices alone have risen by around ₹9 a litre following the West Asia crisis, observes Sabu, who operates three buses.
An interesting anecdote about Kerala’s private bus industry is closely intertwined with the State’s enduring tea culture. Sunil Kumar, owner of Saroma Travels, which once operated a fleet of 10 buses but now runs only four services in Thiruvananthapuram city, recalls the long-standing relationship between the price of a cup of tea and the minimum bus fare. “When I entered the industry in 1994, the minimum bus fare was ₹1, and a cup of tea too cost ₹1. By 1996, both had risen to ₹2, and they continued to rise together at regular intervals,” he recalls.
Just before the introduction of the Priyadarshini scheme, the minimum private bus fare in Keralam was ₹10, so was the price of a cup of tea. But things changed after the West Asia war. While the tea prices rose to ₹15 across the State, the minimum bus fare remained unchanged despite a sharp increase in fuel prices and other operational costs, including price of spare parts and accessories.
“Besides these increases, the State government’s free-travel scheme came as a body blow to the industry that has already been struggling to survive,” Kumar says.
Private bus revenues have also failed to keep pace with the rise in the consumer price index over the years. The disparity is evident from the experience of Shaji, a bus owner and office-bearer of the Kerala Private Bus Federation. “Fifteen years ago, the minimum bus fare was ₹5, and a single bus generated ₹7,000-₹8,000 in revenue a day. Even today, buses on the most profitable routes earn only around ₹9,000 to ₹10,000 a day. The interesting part is that diesel that cost ₹35 a litre 15 years ago costs ₹104 today. The daily wage of bus crew has risen from ₹300 to around ₹1,100 during the same period,” explains Shaji.
Long day, low wages
The plight of bus crew members is even more distressing. An average crew member begins the day around 5 a.m., with most private buses starting services between 5.30 a.m. and 6.30 a.m. The workday often stretches until 9 p.m. or 10 p.m., making for 12-15-hour shifts.
Crew members who once earned around ₹1,100 to ₹1,200 a day often receive only ₹700 to ₹800 on less profitable routes because of falling revenues.
Rajesh G., who has worked as a private bus conductor on the Irinjalakuda-Triprayar route for the past 24 years, says the demanding work schedule bears little relation to the remuneration. “The only reason many of us continue in this profession is that we do not possess any other skills or means to support our families. During the COVID-19 pandemic, I tried selling lottery tickets on the streets to make a living, but the income was not enough to support my family. That eventually forced me back into the only profession I know,” Rajesh sighs.
Happy women
On the other hand, the latest turn of events has brought cheer to women across Keralam, although the major beneficiaries of the free-ride scheme are those in southern Keralam and parts of central Keralam. According to Deepa M., a native of Kallambalam and a private-sector employee, the scheme has been a boon, particularly for women working in low-paying jobs in textile shops, sales and other unorganised sectors. “Saving an average of ₹1,000 to ₹1,800 a month means a lot to an ordinary homemaker,” she feels.
However, she points out that the scheme has its drawbacks too. “My son studies in a school in Sreekaryam, Thiruvananthapuram. He travels from Kallambalam to Sreekaryam, a route where KSRTC enjoys a virtual monopoly. Student concession is available only on KSRTC Ordinary buses, which are now overcrowded with women passengers, forcing him to travel on KSRTC Fast Passenger buses, which do not offer student concession. Whatever I save through the free-ride scheme is lost on my son’s daily commute,” Deepa says.
The major grievance of private bus operators is the manner in which the State government implemented the scheme without introducing measures to shield the private bus sector from its adverse impact. The government could have extended the scheme to private buses as well. An income-based scheme applicable to both the KSRTC and private buses would ensure that economically weaker sections continue to receive the benefits while also supporting the student community, feel bus operators.
“Such a model would reduce pressure on routes inadequately served by the KSRTC and enable the State to extend the benefit to people across Keralam by making optimum use of the existing public transport network,” feels Gopinathan.
An expert committee headed by former Transport Commissioner K. Padmakumar has submitted a report to Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan recommending several measures to address the concerns of private buses numbering around 11,000, including according the sector industry status. However, private bus operators have rejected most of the recommendations, saying they do little to address their immediate concerns.
The road ahead remains uncertain for the private bus operators.

briefs.headline: Breaking the blister pack: Counterfeit, adulterated medicines network busted
briefs.deck: Over the year, investigative agencies have busted nine big drug rackets involving counterfeit and adulterated pharmaceuticals, from cancer treatments and vaccines to antibiotics and psychotropic medicines
briefs.bodyText:
Rajkumari and Darshan, both in their mid-30s and from Jharkhand, are leaving Delhi’s All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) after a check-up. They pause to collect themselves before navigating the medical stores outside. Rajkumari hangs on to her husband, who lugs an oversized bag that weighs him down. They have been given a list of medicines to buy.
Rajkumari was diagnosed with blood cancer about 10 months ago and referred to AIIMS for treatment. Since then, the couple has spent a large part of its savings on medicines, travel, and staying in Delhi. Darshan says he has sold their land to keep paying for the medicines.
He pulls out her prescription and points to a name. A single injection of the medicine costs around ₹1.5 lakh and his wife will need several vials. The drug is used in the treatment of blood and bone marrow cancers, including multiple myeloma. It is also among the high-value cancer medicines that figure in an investigation by Delhi Police’s Inter-State Cell into counterfeit and illegally diverted drugs. The racket, spread across Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Telangana, was busted in late August.
Aditya Gautam, Deputy Commissioner of Police, Crime Branch, says Delhi Police has so far arrested 17 people and recovered 588 filled vials and 3,021 other medicines, all valued at about ₹9 crore. “Investigators found original cartons and empty boxes being retained and reused. Batch numbers, MRP details, and other identifying marks were allegedly removed with chemicals like acetone before the medicines were repackaged,” he says.
“Investigators found original cartons and empty boxes being retained and reused. Batch numbers, MRP details, and other identifying marks were allegedly removed with chemicals like acetone, before the medicines were repackaged”Aditya GautamDCP, Crime Branch, Delhi Police
The seized cancer drugs include Darzalex, Imfinzi, Erbitux, Opdyta, Gazyva, Bavencio, Adcetris, and Keytruda. Bavencio and Adcetris have been confirmed as counterfeit by the manufacturers; reports on the others are awaited.
A doctor at AIIMS involved in Rajkumari’s treatment says a red flag for a counterfeit drug is when it shows no results. He also says large discounts on drugs may indicate they are fake.
People pour in from across the country to Delhi for medical treatment.
In 2022, the national capital had nine Joint Commission International-accredited hospitals, meaning they meet global standards of clinical excellence. This is the highest number in the country, making Delhi a medical hub. This also brings with it the problem of counterfeit drugs.
Every month, Delhi Police and the Delhi Drugs Control Department report seizures of medicines they describe as “counterfeit, spurious, adulterated, illegally diverted or unauthorised”.
Substances seized range from basic allergy and skin treatment drugs to high-value cancer medicines, antibiotics, vaccines, and other life-saving pharmaceuticals.
Unless the operations are large, news of these raids and the names of the medicines seized seldom reach people. Tracing a fake medicine to a person is a long and expensive process, so it is seldom done.
Medicine raids
In May this year, spurious oxytocin injections in government hospitals in Rajasthan’s Kota were a major reason for the deaths of five women following caesarean-section deliveries. The same batch of spurious oxytocin had reached Delhi government hospitals too, sources say, after which it was seized by the Drugs Control Department.
Five days after the inter-State drug raid that seized cancer medicines, the Crime Branch, in a separate investigation, arrested Dr. Manish Sharma, 39, a resident of Faridabad in Haryana, for allegedly selling smuggled, suspected adulterated, and counterfeit life-saving drugs.
According to the police, Sharma had gone to Russia to study medicine and returned to India in 2014. He later worked at a hospital in Faridabad before opening his own hospital. After those ventures shut down, he and his wife started a polyclinic in the city. Sharma also registered HK Pharmaceuticals at the same address and began selling medicines on an e-commerce platform.
The police claim that he began sourcing medicines through illegal channels and selling them to buyers online. Last month, the Drugs Control Department seized a counterfeit anti-rabies vaccine worth ₹2 lakh from Chandni Chowk’s Bhagirath Palace. A government official says the department acted on a tip-off and sent the vaccine to a testing centre in Himachal Pradesh’s Kasauli.
The problem of counterfeit drugs is not new. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, the Crime Branch busted a facility allegedly manufacturing fake Remdesivir. At the time, hospitals were prescribing Remdesivir for COVID-19, and families were pooling savings to procure it, with one vial selling for as much as ₹90,000.
In 2022, spurious medicines valued at over ₹5 crore were seized from a factory at Tronica City in Uttar Pradesh’s Ghaziabad district. In 2024, investigators detected vials resembling high-value cancer drugs. Investigators are examining possible links between some of these and the present inter-State network, but no definitive connection has been established so far.
Labels stripped away
According to Crime Branch officials, medicines may reach people in different ways: counterfeit drugs made in warehouses, often made to look genuine; genuine medicines illegally diverted from the chain for which they were procured, such as drugs from a government hospital being diverted to the open market; and unauthorised medicines that are genuine but not legally approved or permitted for sale in India.
Once a medicine is tainted, either because it is spurious or has been removed from its legitimate supply chain, it moves through layers of intermediaries across States. Some are stored in homes or warehouses before being passed on to wholesalers, brokers, and pharmacists.
Paperwork is another layer of camouflage. The police say invoices are generated for medicines that were never actually supplied, creating a paper trail for illicit transactions. In one instance, investigators found amounts routed through a firm’s bank account and, after GST and commission were deducted, the balance returned in cash. Registers and diaries recording medicine transactions and cash dealings were also recovered. The total turnover and profit from the illicit trade are still being worked out.
Medicines typically pass through manufacturers, clearing and forwarding agents, stockists, sub-stockists, and retailers before reaching a patient. Each handover creates an opportunity for pilferage, according to the police.
“Indian laws require purchase and sale records at every stage, but an invoice only attests that a transaction occurred; it does not ensure that the product inside the box matches its label,” says Nilaya Varma, Group CEO of Primus Partners. “That loophole is precisely where counterfeiters operate,” he adds.
Manufacturing and packaging can be particularly difficult to police, he says, because convincing labels, copied batch numbers, holograms, and reused original packaging can defeat visual inspection. At the wholesale level, multiple transfers can further blur a product’s source, allowing suspect stock to mix with genuine medicines. A pharmacist may be able to check the brand and batch number, but cannot establish the history of an individual pack.
Technology has added another layer of protection, but not an infallible one. India has required barcodes or QR codes on around 300 specified brands since August 2023, but a code that is merely scanned is not necessarily proof of provenance. “A copied or cloned code will pass a visual or app-based scan just as readily,” Varma says, arguing that verification against the manufacturer’s own database at the point of sale would provide a stronger safeguard.
The scale of the pharmaceutical market also limits the reach of testing. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and State drug regulators tested 1,16,323 samples in 2024-25, of which 245 were declared spurious or adulterated.
According to the government, more than 960 drug manufacturing premises have undergone risk-based inspections, resulting in over 860 regulatory actions.
Varma says regulators cannot physically examine every pack moving through more than 8.5 lakh retail pharmacies. “Sampling is a backstop that identifies a bad batch after the fact,” he says. “It cannot certify the pack in a patient’s hand at the moment of sale.”
The Crime Branch is still tracing the complete downstream chain, including pharmacies, distributors, end beneficiaries, and the financial trail. The number of patients who may have received counterfeit medicines, and any confirmed adverse health consequences, has not yet been established.
The lowest bidder
The wider supply chain also raises questions about how medicines enter hospitals in the first place. Lower tendering costs are among the causes, say doctors in Delhi, particularly those working in government settings.
“The government should facilitate more sampling and have more testing labs. The onus can only be on the government to make these checks. It isn’t possible for individual hospitals to do actual quality checks”Dr. Sumit RayMedical Director, Holy Family Hospital, Delhi
Hospitals have drug and therapeutics committees that select and regulate the medicines brought into the premises. They point out that government directives require medicines to be procured from the lowest bidder, and if a hospital has not done so, it is expected to explain why.
Dr. Sumit Ray, Medical Director of Holy Family Hospital in Okhla, Delhi, a hospital run by a charitable trust, says the committee he chairs decides which medicines are selected. “It is difficult to prevent such medicines from entering the system, but there can be multiple levels of checks. For instance, if it is a new pharmaceutical company, we check which other hospitals it has supplied to, who its manufacturers are, and what the reputation of the manufacturer is. The packaging and labelling can also throw up red flags.”
He says while it is not a perfect system, hospitals do what they can to ensure that medicines are genuine. “Ideally, the government should facilitate more sampling and have more testing labs. The onus can only be on the government to make these checks. It isn’t possible for individual hospitals to do actual quality checks,” he says.
Dr. Shyam Agarwal, chairperson of the Department of Medical Oncology at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, says when a patient reports that a medicine is not effective, doctors cannot establish whether the medicine itself is to blame.
“One way to avoid counterfeits is to ensure that the supply coming into hospitals is from genuine companies and that they are not offering steep discounts. A 50% discount should raise suspicion,” he says.
A broken chain
While investigations have traced the chain in such cases, the implications for patients are rarely known. Patients find it almost impossible to establish whether they have consumed a counterfeit medicine. In the case of the rabies vaccine, for instance, a government official says, “It is hard to trace how many patients have consumed it, and from where. If we circulate notices warning patients about a particular medicine, it might lead to more panic.”
The official adds that one way to check whether a patient has received a counterfeit medicine is to trace the batch number recorded on the bill.
Patient rights advocate Bejon Kumar Misra points out that there are not enough large-scale studies to ascertain the impact of counterfeit medicines and that even when data is recorded, it is rarely traced back to patients. “One of the major causes of the issue is that the lowest bidder ends up getting preference,” he says.
He adds that while many patients are affected, many do not even realise they have consumed counterfeit medicines and that the medicines are not working.
According to government data, drug regulators tested 1,41,322 samples across India in 2025-26. Of these, 3,012 were declared ‘Not of Standard Quality’ and 283 were found to be spurious or adulterated. State drug regulators initiated 779 prosecution cases for the manufacture, sale, and distribution of spurious or adulterated drugs.
When medicines fail silently
The consequences are most serious when the failure is not immediately visible.
In cancer treatment, a counterfeit or substandard medicine may contain too little or none of the active ingredients needed to work. A patient may continue treatment believing therapy is being administered while the disease progresses. The delay in detecting treatment failure makes oncology one of the areas most affected by counterfeit medicines, Varma says. With emergency or other life-saving medicines, the consequences can be immediate. Incorrect ingredients or contamination can also cause harm independent of the illness being treated.
For the health industry, the damage extends beyond the patient. Manufacturers can face lost sales and complaints over products they did not make; legitimate distributors and pharmacies bear the cost of investigations and recalls; and repeated counterfeit incidents can erode confidence in genuine medicines and India’s pharmaceutical supply chain.
The answer has to move beyond periodic enforcement, Varma says. Manufacturers need tighter accounting of unused and returned vials, hospitals need records of who receives high-value injections and how empty vials are disposed of, and wholesalers and pharmacies need to conduct stronger checks on suppliers and maintain traceable purchase records.
The fear of fake
Every time Jharana Mallick, 32, who has thalassemia, goes to buy iron chelator medicines, she is careful about which company she picks and medical store she buys from, hoping she does not have to relive what happened 10 years ago.
“For a whole year, the medicines I bought from dispensaries had no effect. After five or six tests, I realised my serum ferritin levels were going up rather than coming down. And I simultaneously started developing issues like osteoporosis and even a gall bladder stone,” she says.
Originally from Odisha, she now lives in Delhi and undergoes frequent blood transfusions. Her mistrust extends beyond the medicines to the system itself. “These are supposed to be life-saving drugs, but they are bought at the lowest tendering costs,” says Mallick, who now works with a charitable trust, Sarvesham Mangalam Foundation, focussed on thalassemia awareness and prevention. In a month, she says, people living with thalassemia can spend up to ₹50,000 on drugs.
Doctors never told her that the medicines she took were counterfeit, she says. But the experience left her with a demand that goes beyond her own treatment: the system should stop “compromising on life-saving drugs”.

briefs.headline: Simi Singh: An Ireland dream, a life-threatening detour and the journey home
briefs.deck: Simranjit Singh a.k.a Simi Singh left left India in 2006 to pursue hotel management, found an unexpected second career in cricket, played for Ireland at the 2022 T20 World Cup and then survived acute liver failure. Now, after his wife donated part of her liver to save him, Simi Singh has returned home to Mohali, bringing a remarkable 20-year journey to an end. Yet, his association with cricket…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Simranjit Singh, known as 
Simi Singh
 in Ireland and across world cricket, had already retired in his mind when acute liver failure brought his career to a shuddering halt in 2024. But on Wednesday, he closed the chapter officially, announcing his retirement and bringing down the curtain on a remarkable 20-year association with Ireland, the country he moved to in 2006 to pursue hotel management, only to find a second life in cricket.
Over his two decades in Ireland, the highs were incredibly high, but the lows were devastating as well.
“I played international cricket, represented Ireland in the World Cup (T20), scored a century while batting at No. 8 against South Africa in ODIs and picked up a five-wicket haul as well. Recently, I came to know that I have the best economy rate in ODIs (3.99), with 
Rashid Khan
 second. When I packed my bags and left for Ireland as a teenager, playing cricket was not something I had in my mind. It was special,” Simi told TimesofIndia.com.
“The people at Cricket Ireland were not surprised because, even before this, I was not being considered for selection. It had become difficult to play professional cricket, especially with my recovery still going on. So I thought it was better to properly close things and make an official announcement so that everyone knew,” added Simi, who played 35 ODIs and 53 T20Is for Ireland.
In early 2024, Simi’s life was turned upside down after he developed a mysterious fever. Doctors in Ireland were unable to find the underlying cause and his health began to deteriorate. He eventually moved to India in search of better medical opinions, only to discover that he had developed acute liver failure. His wife, Agamdeep Kaur, donated part of her liver to save his life.
“My wife is my guardian angel. She was God-sent. She gave me a new life. It was a torrid time for the family,” he said.
“Now I have moved back to Mohali. Recovery is still going on. There is improvement, but it is slow. I will survive,” he added.
It was never all hunky-dory for Simi in Ireland. With tough residency rules, his ECB Level 2 coaching qualification and certification as a personal trainer helped him stay afloat before he eventually broke into the national team. Now, the coaching qualification he earned all those years ago has come to the fore. He has opened his own cricket academy in Mohali, the city where he toiled during his formative years and represented Punjab successfully at the U-14 and U-17 levels.
“For now, I am not running the academy myself. I have completed Level 2 with the England Cricket Board, and I am thinking of doing Level 3. Then we will see what opportunities come up,” he said.
When Simi left India in 2006, he was frustrated that his cricketing career had failed to take off. Nearly two decades later, the 39-year-old looks back at his journey with a sense of gratitude — or shukrana, as he puts it in Punjabi.
“I am relaxed here. My parents are fine. My dad even came to the ground with me. It is good to be back home. My parents were getting old. I am not missing any festivals. Now the coming and going and all that headache is over,” he said.
For someone who left India as a teenager without cricket even figuring in his plans, Simi’s journey has come full circle. Ireland gave him a career he had stopped believing was possible. Then he fought a life-threatening illness but his wife gave him a second chance at life. Now, with cricket behind him as a player, Simi wants to build the next chapter from Mohali, closer to home and with a renewed sense of gratitude.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026 India’s medallists: Full list of winners
briefs.deck: Here’s the full list of Indian medallists at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 categorised by sport
briefs.bodyText:
The 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games are underway in Japan. India is currently placed at the 8th spot on the medals’ table with 66 medals. China is leading the table with 290 medals. Japan is second with 218 medals and Republic of Korea is third with 113 medals.
Compound archer Ganesh Mani Ratnam Thirumuru won men’s individual bronze
India’s Dharmveer Chaudhary, Manu T.S., Jay Kumar and Vishal T.K. clinched the bronze medal in the men’s 4x400m relay at the Asian Games.
India’s Sunil Kumar clinched bronze in the Greco-Roman 87kg category at the Asian Games 2026, becoming the first Indian Greco-Roman wrestler to win two medals at the Games.
Kynan Darius Chenai and Neeru Dhanda staged a superb comeback to beat Qatar and claim gold in the trap mixed team event. The Indian pair finished with an Asian-record score of 34, securing India’s third gold medal of the day.
India edged China 238-237 to clinch gold in the men’s compound archery event, completing a clean sweep of all three compound events. Earlier, the women’s team of Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Prithika Pradeep and Chikitha Taniparthi defeated China to win gold, while India beat South Korea in a shoot-off in the mixed team final to seal another gold and secure a place at the LA 2028 Olympics.
Indian boxer Priya Ghanghas signed off with a bronze medal after going down to former world champion China’s Yang Chengyu in the 60kg semifinal and similarly, Kapil Pokhariya bowed out with a bronze medal after losing 1-4 to Uzbekistan’s Turabek Khabibullaev in the men’s 90kg semifinal.
On Tuesday (September 29, 2026), the quartet of Kiran Pahal, M.R. Poovamma, Prachi Choudhary and Vithya Ramraj won India’s first and only track-and-field gold medal at the Asian Games in Nagoya.
Indian boxer Narender Berwal won the men’s +90kg bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games after losing to reigning world champion Aibek Oralbay of Kazakhstan in the semi-finals on Tuesday (September 30, 2026).
Gulveer Singh added a third medal to his tally at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, clinching bronze in the men’s 5000m on Tuesday.
India’s mixed 4x100m relay quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha S.S., Animesh Kujur and Harita Bhadra clinched bronze at the Asian Games.
India’s Pooja Singh secured the bronze medal in the women’s high jump at the 2026 Asian Games on Tuesday after clearing 1.84m in the final.
The quartet of Manu T.S., Dharmveer Choudhary, Jay Kumar and Vishal T.K. clinched bronze in the men’s 4x400m relay final on Tuesday.
Neeru Dhanda scripted history on Tuesday (September 29, 2026), becoming the first Indian shooter to win an Asian Games gold medal in the women’s individual trap event, while also breaking the continental record in the process.
Indian shooters Neeru Dhanda, Aashima Ahlawat and Manisha Keer clinched silver in the women’s trap team event at the Asian Games.
On September 28, 2026, Vithya Ramraj won a bronze medal in 400 M hurdles in a sensational run that clocked 54.75 seconds and broke her own national record she had jointly held with athlete PT Usha.
Murali Sreeshankar and Gulveer Singh claimed silver medals in the long jump and 1500m, respectively, while Parul Chaudhary secured bronze in the women’s 5000m, adding a second medal to her Aichi-Nagoya campaign.
India also bagged two medals in the javelin throw, with Yash Vir Singh winning silver and Rohit Yadav taking bronze, behind Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga.
Earlier that day, Indian shooter Esha Singh clinched a silver medal in the women’s 25m pistol individual competition.
Pincky Balhara became the first Indian to win two Kurash medals at the Asian Games after clinching bronze on Monday (September 28, 2026), following a 0-5 semifinal defeat to South Korea’s Sumin Mo in the women’s 78kg event.
On Sunday (September 27, 2026), India’s Abhay Singh settled for an Asian Games silver medal after going down against Eain Yow Ng of Malaysia in the men’s singles final of the squash competition, and junior world champion Anahat Singh similarly secured a hard-fought Silver in the women’s singles final against Malaysia’s Sivasangari Subramaniam.
Harita Bhadra clinched bronze in the women’s 200m at the Asian Games. Long jumper Ancy Sojan secured silver in the women’s long jump, while Sarvesh Kushare claimed silver in the men’s high jump.
Tejaswin Shankar, meanwhile, secured his second Asian Games medal, winning bronze in the decathlon following the two-day competition.
Parul Chaudhary bettered her personal best on her way to bronze in the women’s 3000m steeplechase at the Asian Games.
On Saturday (September 26), India’s Sawan Barwal won a silver medal in the men’s marathon. India’s women’s kabaddi team extended their dominance at the Asian Games securing yet another gold medal after a thrilling 37-34 win over Iran in the finals. The men’s hockey team continued it’s winning streak, defeating Japan by 2-0, securing the semifinal berth in the big-ticket sports event.
Simultaneously, the squash squad led by teen-sensation Anahat Singh and Abhay Shetty in singles category stormed into the final game. The duo will be competing for a gold medal in their final game on Sunday.
Women’s 50m rifle 3P team comprising of Vidarsa Vinod, Ashi Chouksey, Tilottama Sen won the silver medal. Mixed squash doubles team including Joshana Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar clinched the bronze medal.
On Friday (September 25), the duo of Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a historic bronze medal in table tennis mixed doubles after stunning the world No. 4 pair from Hong Kong to enter the semi-finals.
Baranica Elangovan entered her name in the record books by winning a historic bronze medal for India in the women’s pole vault event at the Asian Games
Indian long-distance runner Gulveer Singh upgraded his Asian Games medal from bronze to silver in the men’s 10,000m.
India’s Manpreet Kaur clinched the bronze medal in women’s shot put competition of the Asian Games with an effort of 17.17m in Nagoya on Friday (September 25).
Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh won gold in the mixed team 10m air pistol event. The Indian team, comprising Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, Rudranksh Patil and Niraj Kumar, won silver in the men’s 50m rifle 3P team event.
The Indian 4x400m mixed relay quartet of Vishal T.K., M.R. Poovamma, Manu T.S. and Vithya Ramraj earned a silver medal in the final at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium.
Manpreet Kaur clinched a bronze medal in the Women’s Shot Put final with a season-best throw of 17.17 meters.
The duo of Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a historic bronze in Table Tennis Mixed Doubles after stunning the world No. 4 pair from Hong Kong to enter the semi-finals.
Seema Kumari, competing in her first Asiad, won a bronze medal in the 10,000m at the Asian Games, 16 years after Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut’s historic gold-silver double in 2010.
Manipur’s Naorem Roshibina Devi won her third consecutive Asian Games medal, clinching silver after losing to Zhang Xiaoyu in the women’s 60kg wushu final on Thursday (September 24, 2026).
Jay Meena secured India’s first-ever soft tennis medal at the Asian Games, fetching a bronze after losing to Japan’s Takuya Kurosaka in the men’s singles semifinals. Star Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu completed her medal collection, winning a silver medal in the women’s 49kg event in the Asian Games.
Lakshya Sen and Ayush Shetty faltered against higher-ranked opponents as the Indian men’s team concluded with a bronze medal after losing 1-3 to their rivals, China, in the semifinals.
The Indian Women’s Cricket Team clinched a historic victory at the Karogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Aichi. Facing off against Sri Lanka in a high-stakes final, the Women in Blue triumphed to secure India’s very first gold medal of the tournament.
Meanwhile, shooters have led the charge for India. The women’s skeet team, comprising Raiza Dhillon, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal, won a bronze with a combined score of 331 here on September 23, 2026.
Experienced rifle shooter Elavenil Valarivan played a starring role in the country’s double-silver haul in the women’s 10m air rifle competition. Elavenil, one of India’s most accomplished rifle shooters, helped the country secure silver in the team event along with Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod. She then went on to add an individual silver.
For the men’s side, teenager Himanshu Dhillon produced a superb performance to win silver, while former world champion Rudrankksh Patil clinched bronze as India secured two individual podium finishes in the men’s 10m air rifle event. The two then teamed up with Parth Mane to win another silver in the team event, finishing just behind China.
After an impressive start in shooting, India also managed to script history in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), with Suchika Tariyal winning the nation’s first-ever bronze medal for MMA at the Asian Games.
A contingent of 501 Indian athletes, comprising 267 men and 234 women, is competing across 36 disciplines in the 2026 edition. Apart from shooting, athletics and archery too are expected to add to the medal tally. India is also defending both the men’s and women’s titles in cricket and kabaddi.

briefs.headline: French school protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest
briefs.deck: The Interior Ministry said police and gendarmes had made 1,949 arrests, while 305 officers had been injured
briefs.bodyText:
French students set fire to bins and erected blockades outside schools in several cities, protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.
Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools on Thursday (October 1, 2026), according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.
Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycées, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France.
The Interior Ministry said police and gendarmes had made 1,949 arrests on Thursday (October 1, 2026), while 305 officers had been injured.
According to Interior Ministry figures, 1,027 lycees of the 3,700 across France had been affected by the movement’s actions, with blockades at 222 of them.
The authorities in the Paris region said around 50 schools had been “the scene of violence, clashes and damage”.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he described as “unbridled violence”.
The office of Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the demonstrations had become “urban violence” and cited the intelligence service to justify claims that it had been organised by the radical left.
Manuel Bompard, a leading figure in the hard-left France Unbowed party (LFI), quickly dismissed the claim, accusing the government of “sinking into conspiratorial thinking” in comments to AFP.
LFI leader Jean-Luc Melenchon demanded to know which arm of the intelligence service had said that.
This latest wave of social unrest comes with tensions already running high over inflation, particularly soaring fuel prices — and just seven months away from France’s presidential election, where opinion polls suggest far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner.
School staff targeted
Since last week, pupils have staged protests outside schools over a range of grievances. They range from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year’s heatwaves.
The protests have spread across the country from the Paris suburbs.
Riot police have lined up against the students, and the force has launched internal probes after accusations of brutality against three pupils, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.
University students also joined in Thursday (October 1, 2026), blocking access to around 30 campuses, a student union said.
Among reports of school staff being targeted was one incident in the southern port city of Marseille when a school principal and his deputy were splashed with petrol. A journalist with TV channel M6 was attacked at the same school, local officials said.
In the northwestern city of Nantes, firefighters had to intervene to extinguish a fire in the entrance of a high school “following a gathering marked by violence towards staff”, the regional education board said.
Authorities reported violence near high schools, mainly in Nantes, blaming “violent individuals” who “join the students to carry out acts of vandalism”.
In the northeastern city of Strasbourg, trams were ordered to halt to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said.
Conditions ‘unbearable’
Raphael, a 17-year-old who did not give his surname for fear of reprisals, was among the protesters outside a school in Strasbourg, where some used barriers to obstruct the nearby tramway tracks.
“There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35°C in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” Raphael said.
“The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors,” he said.
Nearby, students took photos of themselves in front of burning rubbish bins, holding up the sign with their school’s name ripped off the tram stop.
In the southern city of Toulouse, hundreds of young people flooded the tram tracks, some toppling trash cans and starting fires, hurling projectiles or smashing bus shelters, AFP journalists said.
In the northern city of Lille, AFP reporters saw young people wearing black hoodies destroy the glass of a bus stop. Firefighters intervened to put out the flames on upturned dustbins set on fire.
The government has accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the protests.
But LFI’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Melenchon, said on Wednesday (September 30, 2026) that his party “called for non-violent methods of struggle”.
In neighbouring Belgium, there were protests and damage at a handful of schools in the eastern city of Liege, police said.

briefs.headline: PNG Drive 3.0 targets 50 lakh new connections, shifts focus to gas network utilisation
briefs.deck: The third phase of the National PNG Drive would be in force until end of fiscal year 2027.
briefs.bodyText:
Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, along with the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) and city-gas distributors, on Thursday launched National PNG Drive 3.0, stepping up efforts to accelerate the shift towards piped natural gas (PNG) for households.
The latest phase, which will run until the end of FY27, targets 50 lakh new domestic PNG connections, conversion of 40 lakh existing connections into active consumers and onboarding another 50 lakh domestic PNG registrations.
The initiative builds on the second phase, which ran from January 1 to June 30, 2026, and added around 13.4 lakh billed connections, while generating more than 15.3 lakh domestic PNG registrations.
PNGRB data showed a sharp acceleration in adoption during the second phase. Average daily additions of domestic PNG connections rose 43% to 6,690 from 4,702, while daily additions of billed consumers increased more than two-and-a-half times to 7,392 from 2,781.
The third phase would focus on improving utilisation of existing city-gas infrastructure. The government also plans to accelerate PNG adoption in newly connected areas, particularly semi-urban and rural markets.
According to PNGRB, around 6.9 lakh inch-km of pipeline infrastructure has been laid across the country, including approximately 2.5 lakh inch-km of steel pipelines and 4.42 lakh inch-km of MDPE pipelines. This network has the potential to support around 1.3 crore domestic PNG connections.
In a social media post, Mr. Puri said “this will strengthen India’s vision of increasing the share of natural gas in the primary energy mix from around 6% currently, while providing a cleaner, reliable and affordable energy source.”

briefs.headline: CJP to protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai on October 2, Dipke challenges CM Fadnavis
briefs.deck: Abhijeet Dipke said that since a large number of people were affected due to the deletions, many will hit the streets; “If Gyanesh Kumar doesn’t resign, they will seek Narendra Modi’s resignation,” he said, alleging that Mr. Kumar was winning elections for Mr. Modi.
briefs.bodyText:
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke said on Thursday (October 1, 2026) that the group will hold a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on Friday (October 2). The protesters’ main demands include the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the filing of criminal charges against him.
CJP has also sought that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) roll be frozen and that the process to appoint the Chief Election Commissioner be made transparent with civil society participation. After Mumbai, the group will hold protests in six other cities, concluding at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi by the end of October.
‘CEC is a traitor’
“Gyanesh Kumar is a traitor. He doesn’t deserve to be the CEC. He is a puppet of Amit Shah and Narendra Modi. There have been 13 crore deletions in the voters’ list since 2024. The gap between the NDA and INDIA bloc was a mere 2% (in the 2024 elections), whereas they got rid of 14% of the vote share. There is an illusion of democracy in the country, and no actual democracy,” Mr. Dipke said.
He added that since a large number of people were affected due to the deletions, many will hit the streets. “If Gyanesh Kumar doesn’t resign, they will seek Narendra Modi’s resignation,” he said, alleging that Mr. Kumar was winning elections for Mr. Modi.
Expressing apprehension about Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), he alleged that all electronic machines can be hacked and demanded that elections be held using ballot papers.
Responding to Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis’ statement about three days’ police custody for protesters, he said he did not mind three months’ custody either. “I want to tell Mr. Fadnavis, mi punha yein (‘I will come back,’ a reference to Mr. Fadnavis’s past statement claiming he would return to power).”
No permission for protest
Meanwhile, the Mumbai police have not given permission for the CJP protest. The Bombay High Court decides on petitions seeking permission to hold public events at Shivaji Park. The designated area for protests in the city is Azad Maidan. When asked if the group had approached the High Court to seek permission, Mr. Dipke said: “What will happen in the court? Taareekh pe taareekh (referring to prolonged court hearings).”
Responding to questions on why he did not choose to protest at Azad Maidan, he said: “We can protest anywhere. We want to protest at Shivaji Park only.”
‘SC equally guilty’
When asked why the group did not wait for the Supreme Court to hear the pending petitions about the problems with electoral rolls and the SIR, he accused the apex court of being equally guilty. “Which Supreme Court? The same court which did not allow people to vote in the West Bengal elections?” he asked.
Responding to allegations of being a B team of the Congress, Mr. Dipke said, “Sit together and decide whose B team we are. The Congress accuses us of being a B team of the RSS and BJP. The ruling party accuses us of being a B team of the Congress.”
IIT student death
Mr. Dipke was asked a question about reservation in education. While responding, he asked why nobody questioned management quota reservation. He said it was shameful that the parents of the IIT Bombay student who died by suicide had to sit on a protest to seek justice.
“Many students have died in IITs. Is there enough representation? There is not. People need to be made to feel that they belong there. How can you justify that a kid can die by suicide for cheating? How inhuman can you become? Children coming from tribal areas have to go through a lot to be at such places. That the parents continue to sit on a protest to seek justice for their child is shameful,” he said.

stories.headline: SIR: Pre-filled Form-7 applications against Muslim voters in Kodagu came from ‘party office’, say objectors
stories.deck: Across multiple Assembly constituencies in Karnataka, pre-filled Form-7 applications were filed in bulk seeking deletion of Muslim voters’ names
stories.bodyText:
In a similar trend seen across multiple Assembly constituencies in Karnataka, where pre-filled Form-7 applications were filed in bulk seeking deletion of Muslim voters’ names, at least 50 applications were filed against Muslim names at a single polling station at the Government Higher Primary School at Bydagotta in Kodagu district on September 23 alone. The objectors said the forms had been sent from the “party office”. All the applications cited “absent” as the reason for deletion.
Data accessed by The Hindu shows that at least 50 Form-7 applications were filed by objectors named Rajni, B.N. Basavaraju, Lokesh, Savitha Malali, and A.C. Nagaraj. However, officials in Somwarpet where the polling station is, said they had not received any of these applications.
When contacted by The Hindu, Mr. Basavaraju and Ms. Rajni said they had filed 10 applications each, claiming they had “doubts” that the voters had “duplicate” entries.
Asked why “absent” had been cited as the reason when they had claimed the voters had duplicate entries, the objectors said they did not know the details and had followed instructions from the party office in Somwarpet.
They further declined to name the party but added that five people were given 10 forms each. “We had doubts that these people have duplicate votes, so we told BLOs that we want to fill Form-7 and filled it offline,” Mr. Basavaraju said.
However, it is to be noted that the forms were already printed with the voters’ names and EPIC numbers, similar to applications seen in other constituencies.
From June 16 to September 24, a total of 61,130 Form-7 applications were filed across the State.
