stories.headline: Karnataka CEO’s order ends 6-hour dharna by CM over alleged voter deletion
stories.deck: Karnataka's Chief Electoral Officer, V Anbukumar, has directed electoral registration officers to launch a probe into claims of false information on voter registration applications. This initiative prompted Chief Minister DK Shivakumar and fellow protesters to conclude their demonstration, which was aimed at urging an inquiry into the deletion of voter registrations.
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) V Anbukumar Thursday directed electoral registration officers (EROs) across 224 assembly constituencies in 
Karnataka
 to initiate legal action against applicants who knowingly submit false declarations in electoral roll application.
This follows a six-hour dharna by chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 and his cabinet colleagues over alleged attempts to delete eligible voters through bulk filing of Form 7 applications during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
Ministers, Cong netas join dharna
Congress called off the protest following the order. Shivakumar said: “It is a historical day for us. Our protest won’t stop till we can take it to a logical end.”
The directive came after a day-long high drama at the CEO’s office, where Shivakumar staged a dharna from 2.45 pm until around 9 pm, demanding a criminal case and a probe into the alleged mass filing of applications seeking deletion of voters’ names. Congress state unit president BK Hariprasad, former CM Siddaramaiah and several legislators and MPs had also joined the protest.
Anbukumar directed EROs to initiate action under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, against applicants found to have knowingly made false declarations in Forms 6, 6A, 7 and 8. However, he said officials must conduct an inquiry under Rule 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, before initiating action.
It was followed by allegations by Shivakumar at a press conference that bulk-filing fake Form 7 applications, which are used to object to the inclusion of names in electoral rolls or seek their deletion.
Shivakumar , who cancelled a scheduled Cabinet meeting, alleged 50 lakh eligible voters had been targeted during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. He claimed minorities, Dalits and backward-class voters were particularly vulnerable to the alleged exercise.
Accusing BJP and JD(S) functionaries of involvement, he demanded that the Election Commission identify and prosecute those responsible. “They have attempted to steal the voting rights of electors. This is vote theft,” he said.
Shivakumar alleged that preprinted Form 7 applications carrying voters’ names, addresses and EPIC numbers had been filed in bulk in Vijayapura, Bhalki, Belagavi, Mysuru, Mudigere and Bengaluru between Sept 22 and 24. He claimed BJP functionaries were involved at more than 70% of booths.
After submitting a memorandum to Anbukumar, the chief minister remained at the CEO’s office, insisting that action be initiated. The Cabinet meeting scheduled for 3pm at Vidhana Soudha was cancelled.
“Protecting the rights of the state’s voters is more important than anything else. This responsibility rests on me,” Shivakumar said before the dharna ended.
The CEO had initially sought time until Friday to examine reports from deputy commissioners, who also function as district election officers, and take appropriate action. Shivakumar said the state government would explore the legalities of a police investigation, adding that affected voters had already filed complaints and FIRs at several police stations.
Citing alleged instances of bulk filing, Shivakumar earlier alleged that some individuals had submitted 84, 92, 241 and 423 applications each and questioned how they had obtained the electoral data.
In Vijayapura City, around 14,000 applications were allegedly filed by BJP workers and staff linked to a BJP legislator’s office, he claimed. In Babaleshwar, six people allegedly filed more than 1,600 applications before withdrawing them after officials warned of legal action. In Bhalki, he alleged that 36 BJP workers had filed 3,244 forms in a single day.
Shivakumar said affected voters had approached the police alleging forgery and that documents and videos relating to Mysuru, Belagavi and Bhalki had been submitted to the Election Commission. He alleged that an organised network had accessed voter data.

stories.headline: Customs slaps Rs 271 crore penalty on Harshavardini Ranya, 3 others in gold smuggling case
stories.deck: Customs authorities in Bengaluru imposed significant penalties on Ranya Rao and three associates for gold smuggling. The penalties amounted to over Rs 270.8 crore for their involvement in illicit activities. Authorities seized more than 14kg of gold from Ranya after her arrival from Dubai, and evidence linked her to prior smuggling operations. Searches at her residence uncovered cash and…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Customs has imposed penalties totalling Rs 270.8 crore on actor Harshavardini Ranya aka Ranya Rao and three others, holding that they were part of a gold-smuggling syndicate that brought more than 127kg of the yellow metal worth Rs 102.5 crore into India between March 2024 and March 2025.
Harshavardini Ranya case
In an order issued on Sept 30, Sandeep Gunjal, the joint commissioner, airport, Bengaluru, held Ranya responsible for the entire consignment and imposed a Rs 102.5-crore penalty on her. Tarun Konduru Raju was fined Rs 62.1 crore, while Sahil Sakariya Jain and Bharath Kumar Jain were each fined Rs 53.1 crore.
The case stems from the seizure of 14.2kg of gold worth Rs 12.6 crore from Ranya on March 3, 2025, after she arrived in Bengaluru from Dubai. The gold was concealed around her calves and waist, in her trouser pockets and inside her shoes.
The order described Ranya as the prime accused. Customs further alleged that Raju handled documentation and the handover of gold on the Dubai side, while Sahil and Bharath were involved in disposing of the gold in India and arranging payments through hawala transactions.
A subsequent search of Ranya’s Lavelle Road residence yielded nearly Rs 2.7 crore in cash and jewellery and other valuables worth Rs 2.1 crore. 
Customs ordered confiscation of the seized gold, cash and other items, maintaining those were proceeds from the sale of smuggled gold.
The larger case involves 14 earlier smuggled consignments totalling more than 113kg of gold, which could not be physically seized by Customs.
The adjudicating authority said it relied on more than 16 hours of airport CCTV footage, 152 documents and other digital and financial evidence while passing the order.
The four can appeal against the order before the Commissioner of Customs (Appeals) within 60 days of its communication.

stories.headline: Karnataka prepares for power supply during summer as consumers grapple with outages
stories.deck: Power demand stood at 298 million units on September 30, lower than the level recorded a few weeks ago
stories.bodyText:
As complaints of power cuts continued to pour in from various parts of the State, including Bengaluru, Energy Department officials said the department has scaled up power supply by more than 3,000 MW to meet the additional load through various sources, including thermal power, procurement from the central grid and independent power generators.
According to the State Load Dispatch Centre, power demand stood at 298 million units (MU) on September 30, lower than the level recorded a few weeks ago. In early and mid-September, power demand had reached 340 MU.
An official said, “The power demand might have reduced due to the good rains received in the past few days. However, we are in a better position in terms of power supply when compared to other States in South India. Power disruptions might be due to overloading, line clearance and even maintenance works at substations that go on for a day.”
However, consumers argued that power cuts are frequent. A resident near HAL in Bengaluru said, “Recently, the Energy Minister said there would be no load-shedding for now. However, in the last few days, power cuts have been rampant in our area. I have lost count of the number of times there have been power failures in our apartment complex. We are managing only because of our generator backup.”
Girijamma, a resident of Rajajinagar, said, “For two days, power supply was unavailable from 10 a.m. and resumed only after 2 p.m. My son has to work from home and with such power cuts, it is difficult. When we call the helpline number, they say it is due to maintenance work.”
There were similar complaints from other districts too
Sanjay Zirali, a resident of Belagavi, said, “I run a small clinic and power disruptions for two to three hours in the evening are a major problem as it becomes difficult to treat patients. I am planning to install an inverter or UPS.”
Power demand
Meanwhile, Minister for Energy and Tourism K.J. George said on Thursday that the State is fully prepared to meet electricity demand in the coming months, with plans in place to meet the projected requirement. “As in the past, we are also exploring power procurement through exchange arrangements with Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana,” he said.
Mr. George added, “Apart from State thermal generation, we have procured 2,000 MW of thermal power in recent months. The annual maintenance of KPCL’s thermal units has been optimised to ensure most units remain available for generation. Adequate coal stocks are being built up. In addition, power banking from northern States will be utilised from November onwards, depending on demand, to meet the State’s energy requirements.”
Gaurav Gupta, Additional Chief Secretary, Energy Department, said, “The State is fully prepared to handle the power situation for now and during the upcoming summer months. We know that electricity demand increased by 30% in September, driven by the impact of El Niño. To meet the sharp increase in demand, the State has scaled up power supply by more than 3,000 MW to meet the additional load.”
He noted that from November 1, another 1,000 MW of power would be available as the State would stop returning power borrowed earlier from northern States.
Mr. Gupta added that an additional 230 MW is being taken in advance from other generators. “Another 236 MW has been allocated to the State from the central pool (Eastern Grid). Further, a Section 11 notification has been issued by the Government of India with effect from October 1, which will make more power available in the exchanges,” he said.
Storage power
Mr. George also said Karnataka is taking concrete steps to build energy storage capacity as an important component of its long-term power security strategy. “Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) will provide greater flexibility in managing peak demand and integrating renewable energy into the grid.”
He explained, “Under KPTCL, projects totalling 500 MW/1,000 MWh are at various stages of implementation. KREDL is also pursuing a 250 MW solar project with 1,100 MWh of BESS at the Pavagada Solar Park. In addition, a 900 MWh BESS project comprising 250 MW/500 MWh at Kushtagi and 200 MW/400 MWh at Huliyurdurga is being taken up.”

briefs.headline: Fake currency racket busted: Seven held, 4.3k notes seized in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Chamarajpet police have busted a counterfeit currency racket with the arrest of a seven-member gang and seizure of 4,337 fake Rs 500 notes, a car, eight mobile phones and equipment used to print the currency. The seized notes have a face value of Rs 21.7 lakh.
The arrested have been identified as Sattaiah alias Sathya (47), 
Murugesan
 (52), Govindan (43), Barkath (38), Saravan (47), Lakshmana (46) and Krishna (43). Three are from Hyderabad, 
Telangana
, and four from 
Tamil Nadu
.
Acting on credible information, a team led by police inspector Kiran V intercepted a Swift Dzire (TN-23-AE-7749) near a fuel station close to the BGS Flyover down-ramp on Sept 14 and apprehended two persons. The duo allegedly confessed to circulating counterfeit notes to make quick money. Police seized 3,000 fake notes of Rs 500 denomination, the car and two mobile phones from them.
During interrogation, the duo allegedly revealed they were working with nine others. Police arrested two more persons in Chennai on Sept 16 and three others in Ranga Reddy district, Telangana, on Sept 18.
Further investigation led the cops to a house in Krishnagiri district of Tamil Nadu, where they recovered 1,337 more counterfeit notes. 
They also seized a computer, laptop, laminator, printer, cutting machine, holograms, photocopier and other equipment used to print the fake currency.
All seven accused have been remanded in judicial custody. Police are searching for four others who remain at large.
Learnt from internet
Sathya, who is involved in business activities, was interested in rice pulling and other illegal activities. He allegedly became acquainted with Murugesan, who is in the paint business. Murugesan had visited Govindan’s printing press in Chennai to get wedding invitations printed, and the two became friends.
Over time, Sathya and Murugesan decided to make quick money and hatched a plan to manufacture counterfeit notes. They shared the idea with Govindan and sought to make the notes closely resemble genuine currency.
They searched the internet for detailed information on making counterfeit notes and began buying the required equipment and paper. They practised for nearly six months, initially struggling to produce convincing notes. They later purchased higher-quality equipment and matching ink and eventually succeeded in printing the windowed security thread.
Once they achieved this, they began circulating counterfeit notes in Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Karnataka over the past two months.
Aside from Sathya, Govindan and Murugesan, the other accused helped set up the equipment and dispose of the notes in the market. Police do not yet have an exact count of the notes the gang manufactured or circulated before being caught, a senior officer said.

briefs.headline: Student union polls: Universities direct colleges to begin process in Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: With the cabinet giving its nod for campus union elections, public universities have started instructing affiliated colleges to take steps to begin the election process.
Adikavi Sri Maharshi Valmiki University, Raichur, issued a notification on Sept 21 to colleges to conduct elections. “Govt has framed and issued guidelines to inculcate civic responsibility, accountability and democratic values among students. It has been directed to conduct student union elections in all affiliated undergraduate and postgraduate colleges under the university subject to the guidelines,” read the circular.
“Currently, election code of conduct is in place because of upcoming polls. Once that is completed, colleges can go ahead with the elections. They are extremely important to inculcate leadership and democratic values,” said vice-chancellor Shivananda Kelaginamani.
Bengaluru City University also issued a circular to affiliated colleges. “We will hold a review meeting with college principals on the preparation before they get into it. 
We need to give them some time,” said B Ramesh, vice-chancellor.
Bengaluru North University has directed college principals to mandatorily submit a report regarding the election process.
The elections are being reintroduced after a gap of 37 years in the state. briefs.headline: KC Das staff strike over unpaid salaries, five Bengaluru outlets hit
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: If you’ve noticed the shutters down at KC Das outlets across Bengaluru over the past week, it’s because around 40 employees across five branches have gone on strike over alleged non-payment of salaries, bringing operations to a halt.
KC Das, known for its sweets, savouries and canned rasgullas, once had 20 showrooms in Bengaluru. It is now down to five — on St Mark’s Road, JP Nagar, Malleswaram, Basavanagudi and Rajajinagar — amid a family and corporate governance dispute.
According to Suresh M, general manager of St Mark’s Road branch, employees haven’t received salaries for over eight months. “Since a new senior manager was brought in, there has been disruption in operations. We have not received salaries since Jan. When we raised the issue with our 92-year-old director in Kolkata, we received 50% of our dues. But the remaining amount is yet to be paid,” he said.
“This has led to great difficulties as many haven’t been able to afford basic necessities for their families or pay EMIs. A few women employees have even pledged their jewellery to make ends meet. 
We have great respect for the director and the company, which has taken care of us for so many years. But now, for our own survival, we had to take this step
,” he added.
Suresh said employees had been deprived of other benefits, including provident fund (PF) contributions, for the past couple of years.
The employees, most of whom are from Karnataka, have approached labour department seeking help. “We received a call from an official and are waiting for further communication,” Suresh said.
When 
TOI
 reached out to Shampa Chakravarty, senior manager at KC Das, there was no response.

briefs.headline: 400 colleges, 31 districts: PE teacher’s mission to take Gandhiji to Karnataka’s youth
briefs.deck: Abida has been working for more than 10 years to spread the message of Gandhiji’s life and principles
briefs.bodyText:
Meet Abida Begum, a senior physical education teacher at Government First Grade College in T. Dasarahalli, Bengaluru, who has been visiting government and private colleges across Karnataka to conduct workshops exclusively on the life of Mahatma Gandhi without charging students a single penny.
Ms. Abida has been working for more than 10 years to spread the message of Gandhiji’s life and principles.
She said, “If not a major change, students can get inspired by Gandhiji’s life and may have brought small changes in their lives. From simple aspects such as being disciplined, valuing time and punctuality, and being honest in what they do at college and beyond the classroom, the lessons are endless.”
For Ms. Abida, her father, Aftab Ahmed Khan, was the inspiration behind her efforts to learn and study more about Gandhiji. “He was a Gandhian and, growing up, I was always inspired by him. I thought knowledge must be shared. Hence, in 2016, I conducted a workshop on Gandhiji’s life and principles at the college where I worked in Ramanagara. The word spread and a few more colleges started approaching me to conduct workshops and camps for their students too. By 2026, I have visited more than 400 colleges, both private and government, across all 31 districts of Karnataka,” she explained.
She said, “Recently, I visited a private college in Kagwad, a border taluk in Belagavi district. The college administration was surprised to know that such workshops were being conducted. They said Gandhian thought is the need of the hour, especially for their students.”
Elaborating on why Gandhiji and his thoughts remain relevant even today, she said, “Many youngsters think Gandhiji is not relevant in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Whenever I visit colleges, students question me about his relevance in their lives when technology is evolving on a daily basis. Gandhiji’s principle that honesty is the best policy does not merely mean speaking the truth. It also means doing tasks, whether at home, college or the workplace, with honesty. Self-reliance is another principle that remains relevant even today. Why do you think there are so many start-ups? Because they are working to make the country self-reliant. Non-violence is another reason why the world needs him today,” Ms. Abida explained.
She said, “I never force college administrations to host my workshops. Some do not show interest due to a lack of time, while a majority have agreed to provide me with space to conduct these workshops.”
Two way conversations during workshops
“During these workshops, some students speak about the fake news circulated on social media about Gandhiji. Many students judge him based on such misinformation. In such instances, I clear the air and present facts. I also recommend books on Gandhiji. The next time I visit the same colleges, students tell me about the changes they have made in their lives,” Ms. Abida said.
She also collaborates with the Karnataka Gandhi Smaraka Nidhi and the National Service Scheme, Youth Empowerment and Sports Department to conduct a seven-day State-level Youth Camp. “These camps are based on ‘Human Values through Gandhian Thoughts’. Students who participate are provided accommodation facilities. Through Gandhian thought, I, along with more resource persons, teach them leadership, communication skills, spinning the charkha and making khadi. There are many such activities planned for the camp.”
She has also successfully conducted the Gandhi Vichar Sanskar Pariksha across Karnataka for the past 10 years. It is an initiative of the Gandhi Research Foundation in Jalgaon, Maharashtra, and she is the coordinator for the examination in Karnataka.
She said, “This year, around 8,000 students registered for the examination and only 325 cleared it. Students are given study material and anybody can participate. Different age groups are provided different study material for the examination. It is usually conducted every February.”

briefs.headline: BMTC steps in to support KSRTC, to run 150 additional outstation buses on October 1
briefs.deck: According to an order issued by BMTC on Wednesday, the additional services will be operated from Kempegowda Bus Station and Mysuru Road Bus Station to cater to passengers travelling from Bengaluru to various parts of Karnataka.
briefs.bodyText:

Bengaluru
The Karnataka Lokayukta Police conducted searches at multiple premises linked to four government officials in Bengaluru and Belagavi on September 30 and October 1 following allegations that they had amassed assets disproportionate to their known sources of income.
The searches were carried out by the Bengaluru City-2 and Belagavi-2 units of the Lokayukta Police. briefs.headline: Karnataka’s drive to green data centres
briefs.deck: Karnataka’s new Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026–2031 targets to attain a cumulative data centre capacity of 1 GW (1,000 MW) by 2031, and incentivises adoption of renewable energy and treated water. Shilpa Elizabeth examines its details and implications...
briefs.bodyText:
For four-year-old Johan Arun, who lives in Electronics City, the most recognisable vehicle is a water tanker. Every day, as the vehicle pulls up, Johan alerts the family by announcing the arrival of “tank water”, says his mother.
The apartment, where Johan and his family live, is yet to receive Cauvery water connection, like many others in the area. Tankers running up and down the roads is a familiar sight in this part of the town.
Not far from here, Lakshmamma (name changed) runs a small tea shop. A native of Haveri, she migrated to Bengaluru 22 years ago. She has fond memories of the days when water was available 24x7. “Not the case anymore,” she says. As she speaks, a large water tanker pulls up, parks along the kerb and starts pumping water into the enormous facility near the tea shop. A large compound wall with barbed wires on it stands between the imposing building and the pavement.
Lakshmamma explains who the tall neighbour that towers over her small shop is. “It is a data centre. Came up around six years ago. It seems to need a lot of water. Daily, around 20 such tankers arrive there,” she adds.
Five in Electronics City
At least five data centres are located in Electronics City currently, as per the government records, with a combined capacity of more than 23 MW. According to government data, there are 32 data centres in Karnataka, most of them located in and around Bengaluru. Major clusters include Electronics City, Whitefield, and Devanahalli. Together, they power Karnataka’s AI dreams.
Across the world, however, data centres have been in the eye of the storm, as locals protest against their environmental impact and governments rethink their policies.
In India, the Karnataka government recently introduced a Sustainable Data Centre Policy, with the aim of establishing a globally competitive, sustainable, and well-connected data centre ecosystem in the State.
Impact on environment
Specialised buildings that house servers, data centres earlier powered everyday online services such as websites, emails, instant messaging, and so on. Things started changing drastically as AI entered the picture. The specialised chips or GPUs used for training or running large AI models consume a lot more electricity.
“A traditional, smaller-scale data centre, used for web and standard IT applications, typically requires about 5 to 10 kW per rack. For an AI hyperscale data centre, the numbers can be 30 to 100 kW per rack,” explains Rishika Ranga, senior associate in the Energy & Power team at CSTEP.
More power generates more heat. Cooling systems that prevent computers from overheating can consume large quantities of water when they rely on water-based cooling. On top of this, electricity and water may be required for other functions such as lighting, power backup, security, cleaning and maintenance, and so on. Other impacts of data centres extend to potential noise pollution due to the whirring of machines, localised heat islands and so on.
Karnataka scenario
Of the 32 data centres, one is located in Mangaluru, one in Bidadi and the rest in Bengaluru. Official data pegs the combined capacity of 18 of these at 292.27 MW. There is no government data on the capacity of the remaining 14; Estimates, however, suggest the total installed capacity of all the data centres in the State at around 400 MW.
Water consumption of only 12 out of the 32 data centres in Bengaluru are currently available with BWSSB. The rest potentially rely on alternate sources of water like private tankers.
According to BWSSB records, majority of the 12 have adopted air-cooled and dry-cooling architecture, which helps to keep water demand lower than water cooling infrastructure. The 12 data centres combined are estimated to consume up to 1,964 KLD or 1.964 million litres per day of water at peak capacity. This is equivalent to the daily water demand of around 3,600 households of four people.
In March 2026, acknowledging the environmental costs of data centres, IT&BT Minister Priyank Kharge termed data centres a “necessary evil” and announced plans to develop a sustainable data centre policy. In September, the Cabinet approved the new Sustainable Data Centre Policy 2026–2031.
The new policy
The new policy, which The Hindu has seen, targets to attain a cumulative Data Centre capacity of 1GW (1000 MW) in Karnataka by 2031, and incentivises adoption of renewable energy and treated water.
Data centre units utilising renewable energy exceeding 50% of their total energy consumption shall be eligible for an incentive of ₹0.50/unit, for a period of five years, irrespective of the source of power procurement, subject to an overall cap of ₹1.25 crore.
Charges incurred towards procurement and use of treated water will be reimbursed fully, subject to a maximum of ₹8 lakh per annum. The incentive is applicable for a period of five years from the date of commencement of commercial operations.
The policy also mandates plant‑wise reporting of Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE.)
PUE
While data centres achieving PUE of 1.00 to 1.20 will receive a one-time financial incentive of ₹20 crore, disbursed in the fourth year after demonstrating the prescribed PUE consistently for three consecutive years, those units maintaining a WUE of ≤0.7–1.3 L/kWh for at least three consecutive years will be reimbursed 100% of their water charges, up to ₹30 lakh a year, for two consecutive years.
According to the policy, the government will also undertake mapping of water and energy availability and usage across existing and proposed data centre locations in the State.
“The exercise is essentially to map where the power supply, etc. can be given comfortably. Water is not a major issue, so we are focusing mainly on power and land availability. Wherever we can mobilise power supply, that’ll be in the map. Then we can explore if land, suitable connectivity, and so on are there, and can work on that. It will be like a guide for investors who want to invest in data centres, and will be made public,” explains N. Manjula, Secretary, Department of Electronics, IT, Biotechnology and Science & Technology, and BWSSB chairperson.
Sustainability-aligned policies
Given that the current capacity in the State is around 400 MW and the policy targets 1GW by 2031, Manjula says that the government is being careful that it is not being over ambitious. “We will go step by step and we are being conscious as the focus is to not just add capacity, but also be sustainable. The intention is also to see if one good data centre project can be facilitated in the coastal area. Then it will be a hub for future growth also,” she explains.
Shylesh Muralidharan, sustainability expert and Senior Fellow at Portulans Institute, terms the policy one of the most sustainability-aligned policies he has come across in India. “It is the first I have seen to combine water-use efficiency, treated-water incentives, and resource heat-mapping with tax breaks,” he remarks. “What is refreshing is that sustainability is tied directly to financial incentives. Offering up to ₹20 crore to a data centre that maintains a PUE at or below 1.20, alongside covering the full cost of treated water for five years in a water-stressed metro, applies the right levers,” Muralidharan says.
According to him, the commitment to map water and power availability across the State to guide project siting is a strong point of the policy.
Srinivas Varadarajan, CEO at Mysuru-based Vigyanlabs whose services include micro data centres, too welcomes the policy and calls it the right approach.
Incentive-based
While the policy’s intent has been welcomed, some concerns remain about its reliance on incentives rather than mandating the use of clean energy or treated water.
Noting that efficiency per unit of compute differs from total water drawn, Muralidharan observes, “While Karnataka’s overall renewable base and State-level water metrics are strong, local realities differ—such as dry borewells around Bengaluru. Water stress is a basin- and neighbourhood-level issue, and I hope the resource heat-map incorporates this level of granularity.”
A research done by WELL Labs shows the importance of granular level data.
The team, including hydrologist Shashank Palur, calculated the water consumption of data centres in Bengaluru based on secondary literature. It was found to be only a small fraction of Bengaluru’s total water consumption.
However, the devil lies in the details. Because, in Bengaluru, Palur says, water consumption of data centres is not a macro problem, but a hyper local issue.
“If you look only at the numbers, it doesn’t come across as a big problem. But it is the location of the data centres that makes it problematic. Most data centres are located in areas which do not have piped water supply. They are basically extracting ground water from borewells or buying from tankers. That puts them directly in conflict with the villages or smaller towns, which are reliant on borewells for drinking water,” he explains.
While treated water is an alternative, currently there is no publicly available data on how many data centres are using the same.
Transparent mechanisms
This underscores the need for a more transparent monitoring and reporting mechanism which would mandate data centre operators to publish their consumption numbers.
“It (the new data centre policy) rewards good behaviour handsomely once a project is running, but it does not yet require a project to disclose its water and power draw before approval. Incentivising good behaviour and mandating transparency prior to operations are different tools, and a policy of this scale would benefit from using both effectively,” notes Muralidharan.
Relying solely on metrices like PUE and WUE, which do not give a sense of the percentage of clean energy or treated water used by data centres, is another limitation.
“PUE, which they use as an efficiency metric, is just an industry-standard ratio... It doesn’t tell me how much power the data centre is consuming. It also ignores the carbon intensity of that power consumed,” Ranga explains. “We need clear efficiency standards, not just broad guidelines. We need something more concrete on what happens when data centres don’t meet these efficiency standards,” she adds.
Muralidharan suggests that data centre operators be required to do full disclosure, including projected water draw, power draw, and grid upgrade responsibilities, before approval. He also feels it may be the right time to come up with better metrics.
Alternative approaches
Varadarajan of Vigyanlabs notes that there is no need to build large data centres in every location. “The global assumption has been that data centres need to be large to be economically viable and efficient. But 80% of the countries in the Global South are smaller countries that mostly require smaller data centres. The industry says smaller ones are not efficient, but that is because of the way they have traditionally been designed,” he says.
According to him, Vigyan Labs redesigned the building and components, including using sustainable bricks, reducing cement use by 70%, and developing more efficient air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled ones. “We also developed an indigenous, fully air-cooled FEMTO server for AI and high-computing workloads that uses less than half the energy of comparable systems.”
According to him, the result has been 70% less electricity consumption, half the space requirement, and zero water use, for the same workload.
While not ruling out the need for hyperscale data centres, he calls for rethinking the design and size of datacentres based on actual needs, with sustainability prioritised over greenwashing, regardless of scale.
“Overall, Karnataka should move forward with expanding its data centre infrastructure given the real demand and strong renewable base,” Muralidharan suggests.
“A policy that is this thoughtful about rewarding efficiency can be equally thoughtful about mandating transparency before construction begins. Projects that can withstand public disclosure will move faster with the community as a partner. Karnataka has made most of this choice well, and incorporating early transparency would complete the framework.”

briefs.headline: Bengaluru witnesses driest monsoon in decades
briefs.deck: According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, between June 1 and September 30, the Bengaluru city station recorded 313 mm rainfall with a departure of -236 mm.
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru over the last few days may have been witnessing heavy rainfall, but the southwest monsoon rainfall pattern between June 1 and September 30 reveals a different story. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, during this period the Bengaluru city station recorded 313 mm rainfall with a departure of -236 mm.
While the Bengaluru station recorded a deficit of -236 mm rainfall between June 1 and September 30, the HAL station received 434 mm rainfall with a deficit of -29 mm. The Kempegowda International Airport received 391 mm rainfall, while the deficit for the station is not available.
A post by an X handle said that the city witnessed the driest southwest monsoon in the last 20 years. “The IMD observatory at Bengaluru sees the driest southwest monsoon in 20 years by recording just 313.3 mm of rainfall against an average of 597.7 mm for the period between Jun 1st to 30th Sept. Previously the observatory had recorded 298.3 mm in the SWM season of 2006,” @BngWeather posted on X.
Overall, as per IMD seasonal cumulative rainfall data, Karnataka received 564.6 mm rainfall against the normal 831.8 mm with a departure of -32%.
Among the districts Bengaluru South (earlier Ramanagara) has received the highest deficit with -87%, followed by Kalaburagi and Hassan with -55% and -53%, respectively. Bengaluru Urban district received 258.7 mm rainfall against the normal 452.4mm with a deficit of -43 %.
IMD Officials have attributed the rainfall deficit to strong El Nino, which delayed the onset of the southwest monsoon in Karnataka.
Karnataka has three meteorological subdivisions — Coastal Karnataka, North Interior Karnataka and South Interior Karnataka.
Coastal Karnataka received 2,228.3 mm rainfall against the normal 3,093.9 mm rainfall with a departure of -28 %. North Interior Karnataka received 329.8 mm against the normal 480.8 mm with a departure of -31%. South Interior Karnataka received 433.7 mm against the 678.4 mm with a departure of -36 %.
“As forecast, we are witnessing strong El Nino conditions which has severely impacted the southwest monsoon in the State,” IMD Scientist C.S Patil said.

stories.headline: RBI eases rules for DIIs to buy bank shares

stories.bodyText: NEW DELHI: Mobile covers imported from China could become costlier as India’s trade remedies authority recommended a five-year anti-dumping duty of $72 per 1,000 pieces. The Directorate General of Trade Remedies found that low-priced imports hurt domestic manufacturers, limiting their ability to raise prices despite higher costs. Chinese imports accounted for 51% of Indian consumption during the investigation period of April 2024 to March 2025. Domestic producers struggled with low capacity utilisation.

stories.headline: India’s $600 billion food market grows at 7% CAGR, food processing given importance: Official
stories.deck: Stating that protein was particularly relevant given India’s large vegetarian population, the official said there was a need to meet growing protein requirements.
stories.bodyText:
India’s food market, estimated at $550–$600 billion is growing at 6–7% CAGR, supported by economic growth and urbanisation, Devesh Deval, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Food Processing Industries said.
He said food processing, accounting for nearly 8% of gross value added in manufacturing, is strategically important as it creates greater value for farmers, attracts investment and is the second-highest employment creator in manufacturing.
“The government’s focus is to increase the level of processing across all 16 broad sub-sectors and ensure greater value reaches farmers,” Mr. Deval said on the on the sidelines of Anuga Select India and Anuga FoodTec India 2026 global food & beverages show organised by Koelnmesse in Mumbai.
“Cereals, meat, fruits and vegetables and dairy remain key segments, with India being the world’s second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables and the largest producer of milk. Fisheries, marine products and animal husbandry also receive dedicated policy attention, while healthier and plant-based foods are emerging areas of innovation,” he emphasised.
Stating that protein was particularly relevant given India’s large vegetarian population, he said there was a need to meet growing protein requirements.
Tarun Bajaj, senior consultant, Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), speaking on the occasion, said India exported $53 billion worth of agricultural and processed food products in 2025–26, placing the country among the top 10 exporters globally.
“Despite geopolitical challenges, exports continue to grow, with rice, meat, marine products, coffee and tea among the leading products, while processed food exports are steadily increasing,” he said.
“This growth reflects the development of infrastructure at both the macro and micro levels, supported by conducive government policies and strong performance by farmers,” he said.
Speaking at the show Martina Englhardt-Kopf, Vice Minister, Ministry of Food and Agriculture, Federal Republic of Germany, said “At a time when geopolitical tensions, the pandemic and disruptions to global supply chains have highlighted the importance of resilience and food security, strong regional value chains must go hand in hand with stable, transparent and rules-based international trade.”
She said the conclusion of the India–EU Free Trade Agreement was therefore “an economically significant milestone, creating a market of around two billion people and liberalising trade covering 99.3% of EU and 96.6% of India’s trade value.”
Addressing delegates Silvio Erkens, Minister of Food Safety, Fisheries & Horticulture, Kingdom of the Netherlands, said “The food sector stands at the crossroads of opportunity and responsibility, with climate change, geopolitical instability and energy shortages creating new challenges for food production, trade and processing.”
“This makes international partnerships, innovation and business collaboration essential,” he said.
According to Milind Dixit, managing director, India & SAARC Region, Koelnmesse Pvt. Ltd. India’s food processing industry is entering an important phase of expansion, driven by rising domestic consumption, greater value addition, technology adoption and stronger integration with global markets.
“The sector has already reached around $382 billion in FY25 and is projected to approach $689 billion by FY34, while processed food now accounts for more than 20% of India’s agricultural exports,” he added.

stories.headline: INOX Group scions file for ₹10,000 Crore IPOs each
stories.deck: All the money raised from the IPO will go to the promoters which includes the Jains and Prodair Corporation and its parent Air Products Inc.
stories.bodyText:
The ongoing Initial Public Offer (IPO) rush has got the Gen-Next of Indian conglomerates getting into the mega fund-raising spree. This time, it is the scions of INOX Group who under two different companies have filed IPO draft offer documents to mobilise ₹ 10,000 crore each from the stock market.
The INOX Group’s division was formally settled in November 2021 through a family accord signed by patriarch Devendra Kumar Jain, splitting the near century-old conglomerate between his two sons, Pavan Jain and Vivek Jain.
Pavan Kumar Jain and his son Siddharth Jain as promoters of INOX Air Products along with U.S. firm Prodair Corporation, India’s largest integrated industrial gases company by revenue have filed papers for potential IPO size of approximately ₹10,000–₹11,000 crore (size as per industry and investment banking sources). It will be a 100% Offer For Sale.
The other side is led by Vivek Jain who runs INOXGFL Group as chairman. His son Devansh Jain and daughter-in-law Avarna Jain (daughter of RP-Sanjiv Goenka Group chairman Sanjiv Goenka) as promoters of INOX Clean Energy Ltd, an integrated renewable energy platform, have filed their company’s DRHP with SEBI for an IPO with total issue size aggregating up to Rs. 10,000 crore.
It comprises of a fresh issue of up to ₹8,000 crore and an offer for sale of up to ₹2,000 crore. From the proceeds of the fresh issue ₹6,000 crore will go towards debt repayment and the rest to be used in General Corporate Purpose as per the filings.
INOX Clean Energy has two principal business verticals. Its renewable power generation business called “IPP Business”, comprises an aggregate renewable IPP portfolio of 9.29 GW across India and Africa.
Its solar manufacturing business, under which it currently manufactures solar photovoltaic (PV) modules, has an aggregate operational solar module manufacturing capacity of 6 GW across India and the United States, as of August 31, 2026.
Its solar cell manufacturing capacity is under construction in India and the United States.
On the other hand INOX Air Products is positioned as the largest integrated industrial, medical, electronic and specialty gases company in India by revenue, with a 22.4% market share in FY26, according to the CRISIL Report cited in the DRHP.
Air Products and Chemicals, Inc., through its subsidiary Prodair Corporation, acquired approximately 50% of the Company in 1999 through a joint venture arrangement, following which the Company was renamed INOX Air Products.
All the money raised from the IPO will go to the promoters which includes the Jains and Prodair Corporation and its parent Air Products Inc.

briefs.headline: As inflation bites, shoppers count every penny
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Indians are counting every penny they are spending—blame it on price hikes and inflation. Consumers are becoming value-conscious, trimming budgets for non-essential spends and curbing impulse purchases even amid the festive season when people typically tend to loosen their purse strings.
From packaged consumer goods to gold and fashion, entry-level shoppers are the hardest hit, said industry executives. “The price increases have had an impact and the market is feeling it. When budgets tighten, households put necessities first and push everything else down the list. The slowdown is becoming visible now in mass markets and rural India,” said Umesh Kumar Agarwal, director at Haldiram Marketing. While consumers are not eliminating purchase decisions altogether, they are postponing them and impulse buying has certainly come down, said Anupam Bansal, executive director at Liberty Shoes.
Pressure building up
Data sets show that pressure has been building up on consumers since the start of the year as the war disrupted energy supplies, pushing up prices of fuel and LPG cylinders. A study released by Worldpanel by Numerator (formerly Kantar) on Thursday showed that overall grocery spending declined by 1% in the March quarter with the drop being sharper in rural homes at 5%.
Urban quarterly expenditure declined 4% y-o-y, compared with 14% growth in the previous year. 
Consumer durables, though, gained share of wallet spends, helped by GST cuts.
“Essentials are being protected, while discretionary purchases are facing greater scrutiny. Higher EMI outlays make short-term disposable spend even tighter,” said Manoj Menon, director, commercial worldpanel division.
NielsenIQ’s (NIQ) recent June quarter snapshot showed that about 68% of FMCG categories have seen a decline in volumes, indicating that consumption has slowed down beyond core categories. The impact has been larger in categories such as washing liquids, detergent bars and toilet soaps. Overall volumes declined by 2% in the quarter.
Rising input costs have weighed on magic price points (Rs 5 and Rs 10 packs) across categories, analysts at NIQ said. Companies across segments including FMCG and durables took more than one round of price hikes to cope with commodity inflation. Increase in crude prices has a direct bearing on packaging and logistics costs.
Jayatheertha Chary, managing director at Mother Dairy, said that input costs continue to face inflationary pressure and the company will continue to calibrate its approach accordingly.
“For us going ahead, the focus will be on affordability, distribution and availability rather than looking at price increases,” said Mayank Shah, chief marketing officer at Parle Products.

briefs.headline: Economy may expand 7.3% in July-September, says finance ministry
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The finance ministry Thursday said the growth momentum extended into the second quarter, although at a more measured pace, and the economy may expand 7.3% during July-Sept.
While flagging multiple parameters and high-frequency indicators to argue that growth has been sustained, the ministry’s latest Monthly Economic Report also came with warnings. “…global conditions have turned unfavourable again. Oil prices have spiked in Sept. Global bond yields have moved sharply higher and continued to climb. India’s bond yield has gone up by less but the lower risk premium pressures the Indian rupee although there is every possibility that, over the medium term, investors would appreciate the fundamental reasons behind the lower risk premium on Indian debt.”
It also flagged worries around short-term pressure on Indian assets and the rupee, along with capital flowing towards geographies due to AI.
“At the same time, developed countries are also racing to secure investments to finance their renewed manufacturing aspirations amid increasing weaponisation of global supply chains. Thus, India, as do other developing nations, faces a stiff challenge to attract capital flows. Indications are, however, that foreign direct investment inflows, on a net basis, should do better this financial year than last.”

briefs.headline: Anup Bagchi: ICICI pro who'll steer HDFC Bank
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: For a bank that has long been a training ground for financial-sector talent, there is a certain symmetry in Anup Bagchi becoming the first outsider to head 
HDFC Bank
. The bigger distinction is that the outsider comes from ICICI, an institution whose seniors have long been conscious of playing catch-up with HDFC Bank, first in market capitalisation and later in size.
Bagchi has spent most of his career inside the ICICI group. A chemical engineer from IIT Kanpur, he joined ICICI after an MBA in finance from IIM Bangalore. His first significant assignment at ICICI was the launch of ICICI Direct under ICICI Securities, during the exuberance of the dotcom era. Over more than three decades, he has moved across treasury, retail and wholesale banking, capital markets, wealth management, insurance and digital financial services.
His career has been less about a single specialisation than about moving between businesses. He was CEO & MD of ICICI Securities before becoming an executive director at 
ICICI Bank
 in 2017. At the bank, he first oversaw retail, business and rural banking and later wholesale banking. He was also chairman of ICICI Prudential Asset Management and served on the boards of ICICI Prudential Pension Funds Management and ICICI Home Finance.
Colleagues describe Bagchi as a big-picture manager who prefers to give teams both a destination and a route to reach it. He is a firm leader, but one known for persuasion rather than theatrics. That approach has also shaped his management style. He is regarded as unusually grounded for someone who has occupied senior positions across a large financial conglomerate, holding meetings with executives in the common canteen rather than behind glass doors.
Since June 2023, Bagchi has headed ICICI Prudential Life Insurance. During his tenure, the insurer crossed Rs 10,000 crore in annualised premium equivalent for the first time in FY2025.
There is another, less visible, feature of Bagchi's career: he has tended to travel light. During transfers between ICICI group businesses, he is known to have moved without taking large teams with him.

briefs.headline: Banks, NPCI to ensure MDR not passed on: SBI
briefs.deck: Chairman Setty says bank aspires to increase UPI transactions through Yono to 5cr per day
briefs.bodyText:
SBI chairman CS Setty sees UPI as an opportunity to provide credit lines through Kisan Credit Card, mudra loan, overdraft against mutual funds. He sees UPI with the potential to become a point-of-sale credit platform, with credit made available when customers transact through UPI and vows to work with NPCI and other lenders to ensure that MDR is not passed on to consumers. Excerpts:
How do you see the impact of MDR?
An estimated 96% of transactions will not attract MDR, as person-to-person transactions and person-to-merchant transactions of up to Rs 2,000 are exempt and there are several other carve-outs. We are developing technology to identify these transactions, and it will be ready by Oct 15, when MDR kicks in.
How will banks ensure MDR costs are not passed on to customers?
Banks and NPCI will ensure that MDR is not passed on to retail customers or small merchants through system-driven MDR calculation, merchant classification and transaction-level pricing controls. Awareness campaigns by banks, IBA and NPCI, along with grievance-redressal mechanisms, will further strengthen transparency.
Does MDR give SBI ammunition to regain UPI market share?
MDR should be viewed in the context of sustaining investment in technology, fraud-risk management and capacity building. Two years ago, our UPI volume was below 10 crore transactions a day. Today, we handle around 20 crore transactions daily, representing around 25% of the total ecosystem size. 
Volumes of this scale, which is also increasing exponentially, require continuous investment in technology. We operate the largest proactive risk-management department, which monitors every transaction while building capacity for future growth. MDR should therefore be viewed from this perspective, rather than merely as a revenue item. It would help us invest further in tech and risk management and serve customers better.
Will MDR allow you to offer incentives for using Yono for UPI?
The improvements are not contingent on MDR. We had been investing in the app even before discussions on MDR began. Yono is a comprehensive service application, and we have simplified the payments experience to increase convenience and daily engagement.
Do you see increased use of SBI's Yono app for UPI?
We have revamped UPI on Yono 2.0 and aim to drive greater usage among our customers, including new-to-bank customers. We have 10 crore registrations, of which five crore are active banking users. However, many customers use third-party apps as well. We have simplified the UPI experience on Yono, which currently handles 1-2 lakh transactions a day. Our objective is to increase this to five crore transactions a day over the next two years and position Yono among the top five UPI apps. SBI is already the largest remitter bank on UPI, and we also want Yono to become one of the most preferred apps.
What is SBI's plan for the UPI business?
Our ambition is to build a large-scale, sustainable and customer-centric UPI franchise across the value chain. We aim to consolidate our strong issuer and remitter position, and scale merchant acquiring beyond our existing 60 lakh merchants and approximately 13 crore monthly transactions. We will pursue this across offline merchants, including through UPI QR codes, as well as online merchants. We also plan to offer our customers a seamless, feature-rich and differentiated UPI experience, while deepening engagement with SBI's broader digital services. Together, these will enable SBI to deepen customer engagement and expand its role in India's digital-payments ecosystem.
What is your assessment of the economy up to Sept?
The broader economic momentum remains resilient, with sustained consumption demand supporting credit growth. Retail personal and MSME credit growth has been healthy, while corporate credit has also grown reasonably well, albeit with some moderation. GST collections further reinforce the resilience of the consumption story.
Is the West Asia conflict affecting capex?
Despite the West Asia conflict and the broader geopolitical environment, we have not seen any adverse impact on the capex momentum. Investment activity remains resilient, with project announcements, particularly in sectors such as power, translating into projects, implementation and subsequently the drawdown of credit lines. Even during periods of heightened geopolitical tensions, capex activity has continued, reflecting the underlying strength and resilience of the investment cycle.

briefs.headline: Macro data signals growth: Sept GST jumps 14.7%; auto, UPI, PE-VC stay strong
briefs.deck: GST collections rise 15%, dispatches from top 5 car companies grow in double-digit
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI/MUMBAI/CHENNAI: It turned out to be a strong end to the first half of the year, with GST collections jumping 14.7% to over Rs 2 lakh crore in Sept, amid double-digit growth in dispatches by the country's top automakers. Other indicators also pointed to continuation of economic momentum despite a turbulent global situation, which is putting pressure on cost.
Official data showed that the GST growth in Sept, based on transactions in Aug, was powered by a 26% jump in integrated GST on imported goods to Rs 65,525 crore as higher commodity prices and a weaker rupee drove up the import bill. Domestic collections remained strong, clocking double-digit growth to Rs 1,37,996 crore. Total refunds fell 3%, resulting in an 18% jump in net collections to Rs 1,76,520 crore.
Among the states, Gujarat (17%), UP (11%), Telangana (18%) and Karnataka (12%) reported strong growth. "It is expected that the GST collections will continue to be robust in the festival season, which typically leads to higher consumption across product categories, and may lead to the annual target for the current year being exceeded," said MS Mani, a partner at Deloitte.
Auto sales gain momentum
The five leading carmakers reported double-digit growth in domestic passenger vehicle dispatches to dealers in Sept, ahead of the festive season. Maruti Suzuki posted nearly 37% growth, while Kia recorded the fastest increase among the five at 41%. Retail registrations will show how strongly consumer purchases match the increased supplies during the festive season.
Utility vehicles powered much of Maruti's expansion, with sales rising 62% to 78,911 units. They contributed more than three-fifths of its additional volumes over last Sept. However, growth extended beyond utility vehicles: Its combined mini, compact and mid-size passenger car sales increased 24% to 91,887 units.
Tata Motors remained ahead of Mahindra and Hyundai in domestic passenger vehicle volumes. Its electric vehicle sales, including exports, increased 67% to 15,384 units.
Daily UPI volumes rise
Digital payments activity also stayed strong in Sept, despite lower monthly transaction counts, with daily average UPI value rising to Rs 97,913 crore from Rs 96,205 crore in Aug and IMPS value increasing to Rs 23,530 crore from Rs 22,701 crore, according to NPCI data. Given the fewer number of days in Sept, monthly UPI transaction volume fell to 2,407 crore from 2,451 crore in Aug, while monthly transaction value declined to Rs 29.4 lakh crore from Rs 29.8 lakh crore. IMPS transactions also fell to 35.4 crore from 36 crore.
On a daily basis, UPI transactions increased to 80.2 crore in Sept from 79.1 crore in Aug. IMPS showed a similar increase in daily value despite the fall in monthly transaction count.
PE-VC investments up 21%
In a reversal of trend in private equity and venture capital (PE-VC) investments, the sector recorded a 21% y-o-y jump in CY2026. In first nine months (Jan-Sept), value of PE-VC investments touched $31.7 billion, against $26.2 billion in the same period in 2025. The investments exclude those in the real estate sector. The rise was driven by $6 billion of investments in Sept, including 12 mega deals (more than $100 million) totalling $5 billion, according to data from Venture Intelligence. Sept also recorded the highest monthly investment value in past two years.

briefs.headline: New Chiefs Cleared: RBI okays Bagchi, Saha as CEOs of HDFC Bank, Kotak; ends succession uncertainty
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: It was a day of coincidences in the banking sector. Two private banks, two new CEOs named Anup, both 
ICICI Bank
 veterans, both IIT-IIM alumni, both 55 years old and both from West Bengal.
HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank ended CEO succession uncertainty on Thursday, with RBI clearing new chiefs for the two private sector lenders after their incumbent CEOs decided against seeking fresh terms.
HDFC Bank appointed Anup Bagchi as MD & CEO from Oct 27, succeeding Sashidhar Jagdishan, while Anup Kumar Saha will be Kotak Mahindra Bank chief for three years from Jan 1, 2027, succeeding Ashok Vaswani.
Bagchi, with more than 30 years of experience across retail and wholesale banking, capital markets, treasury and insurance, spent much of his career with the ICICI Group. He was executive director at ICICI Bank from 2017 to 2023, overseeing retail, business/rural and wholesale banking, before heading ICICI Securities. Since June 2023, he has been MD & CEO of ICICI Prudential Life Insurance.
Under Bagchi, ICICI Prudential Life's annualised premium equivalent crossed 10,000 crore for the first time in FY25, while profit after tax (PAT) rose nearly 40% to 1,189 crore.
Bagchi, Saha are both IIT-IIM alumni
Bagchi, the first outsider to lead HDFC Bank since it was set up in 1994, will focus on loan growth, credit-deposit dynamics in a competitive rate environment and extracting synergies from the HDFC merger. 
Jagdishan, who succeeded Aditya Puri in late 2020, led the bank through the pandemic, expanded digital operations and completed the merger.
After RBI approved Bagchi’s appointment and remuneration, the bank’s board will induct him as an additional director from Oct 2, subject to shareholder approval. His term runs to Oct 26, 2029.
Saha, currently a whole-time director at Kotak, joined the bank in January 2026 and has overseen retail banking, data analytics and marketing since March. Before Kotak, he was MD & CEO of Bajaj Finance. He has over 32 years’ experience, including 25 years in financial services.
During his 14 years at ICICI Bank, Saha led retail secured assets, business intelligence, retail and rural collections, credit cards and retail structured finance.
Vaswani had announced he would step down when his term ends in Dec. Kotak chairman C S Rajan said Saha would lead the franchise towards sustainable growth, while Vaswani highlighted his experience across businesses, customer segments and functions. As of June 30, Kotak Mahindra Group had 5,916 branches and a consolidated balance sheet of Rs 10.1 lakh crore. Bagchi is an IIT Kanpur and IIM Bangalore alumnus; Saha holds a BTech from IIT Kharagpur and an MBA from IIM Lucknow.

briefs.headline: Govt. caps sugar stock limit for dealers to 1,000 quintals ahead of festive season
briefs.deck: The Food Ministry said the objective of the amended rules was to “ensure that there is no unnecessary accumulation of sugar in the distribution chain” and that the supply of sugar from mills through dealers to the consumer remained “smooth”
briefs.bodyText:
The government on Thursday (October 1, 2026) tightened the stock-holding limit for sugar dealers to 1,000 quintals, effective from October 15 to November 30, in a bid to ensure adequate supplies at reasonable prices during the festival season.
Dealers will be allowed to hold stock for only 15 days. The amended norms will not apply to Kolkata and its extended metropolitan areas, and Assam, where the limit is 2,000 quintals, the Food Ministry said in a statement.
The new sugar season began on October 1.
“By restricting the quantity and storage period of sugar, the government aims to facilitate the orderly movement of sugar through the supply chain and ensure its continuous availability to consumers at reasonable prices,” the Ministry said in a statement.
Kolkata buys sugar from Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka, and supplies it to eastern India, including the northeast. The limit for Assam takes into account geographical constraints, transportation facilities and consumer interest in the northeast, the Ministry said.
The Ministry said that the objective of the amended rules was to “ensure that there is no unnecessary accumulation of sugar in the distribution chain” and that the supply of sugar from mills through dealers to the consumer remained “smooth”.
In August, citing a tight supply year, the government had imposed a nationwide stock-holding limit on dealers of 4,000 quintals, applicable from August 1 to November 30, along with a maximum holding period of 30 days from the date of receipt. The limit was later tightened to 2,000 quintals from September 15.
According to the Ministry, average retail sugar prices have fallen 15% from their August peak and are expected to decline further as lower prices in the supply chain are realised. Ex-mill prices have dropped by around 28% and have remained stable for the past three weeks.
The government reiterated that mills, dealers, wholesalers and other market participants must ensure uninterrupted movement of sugar and prevent hoarding and speculation. Wholesalers and retailers have also been urged to “immediately pass on” the benefits of the sharp fall in ex-mill prices to consumers.
Sugar mills have been advised to begin crushing operations in line with agro-climatic conditions in their areas. State governments have also been asked to take appropriate action on crushing based on prevailing circumstances.
The Centre will continue to monitor the impact of erratic and inadequate rainfall linked to El Niño conditions on sugarcane in some producing areas, and will take timely measures to balance domestic availability, consumer interest and the interests of cane farmers, the Ministry said.

stories.headline: Gold medal secured! India’s women recurve archers defeat South Korea in final
stories.deck: India made history as its women's recurve archery team bagged the inaugural gold medal at the Asian Games, defeating the formidable South Korean squad, known for their ten Olympic golds, with a tight score of 5-3. The final was a nail-biter, with both teams demonstrating exceptional prowess amidst blustery weather. This landmark win comes after a thrilling semifinal against China, underscoring…
stories.bodyText:
India’s women’s recurve archery team created history on Friday, defeating world champions South Korea 5-3 to claim its maiden Asian Games gold medal.
Ankita Bhakat
, Kirti Sharma and Kumkum Mohod held their nerve in windy conditions to overcome the 10-time Olympic champions in a closely fought final.
Asian Games Full Coverage
 | 
Schedule
 | 
Medal Tally
The opening two sets were evenly contested, with the teams sharing the points after both produced scores of 54 and 56 respectively.
South Korea then faltered in the third set. The Korean trio of reigning world champion Kang Chaeyoung, Oh Yejin and Lee Yunji hit three successive 8s to finish with 52 points.
India capitalised on the opening, scoring 55 to take the set and move ahead.
The fourth set went down to the wire. Korea managed 54 points, while Kirti initially registered an 8 with her opening shot. The score was later changed to 9, taking India’s total to 54.

The Indian team had earlier secured its place in the final by beating China 5-1 in the semifinal, reaching the Asian Games title clash for the first time.

stories.headline: ‘If India won a medal, we owe it to her’: Captain Swayams on Savitha's heroics
stories.deck: Welcome to TimesofIndia.com's interview series looking back at India's medal-winning campaigns at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. After kicking things off with Srinath Narayanan and India's silver-winning Open team, we turn to Swayams Mishra, captain of the bronze-winning women's team. In an exclusive interaction, the 34-year-old opens up about his first full stint as captain, the difficult…
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Across the open and women's sections at the Chess Olympiad, only one player won an individual gold medal for India at the 2026 Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. That was Chennai's 19-year-old Savitha Shri Baskar. Savitha was often the one India could rely on when the team was staring at heartbreak. With her games routinely going down to the wire, she was kept fuelled, game after game, by someone making sure she never had to think about anything other than the board during India's bronze-clinching campaign.
"If we wanted something, he was always there, giving us everything, like water, bananas, and for me, he was bringing endless coffees because I played till the last moment, making sure that I ate properly and got energy," Savitha recalled, before labelling Swayams Mishra as the "best captain ever".
For Mishra, it was new territory in a role he'd long been adjacent to.
"I've been part of the women's team since 2022, but this was the first time I was captaining completely. In 2024, I had captained for a couple of games, but this was a completely new experience," he told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction.
"This time, I have to be there in the tournament hall with the players, especially in the critical games, so the emotions are completely different compared to when you are outside. 
That was slightly different, and not easy."
The coffee, the bananas, and the helplessness of watching
The job, according to Mishra, was less about tactics and more about manoeuvres of a different kind.
"It was hectic and exhausting, because as a captain you try to follow all the games going on, not just one player's. At the same time, sometimes you see a player making a mistake; you want to do something, but you cannot; you just have to wait for it to unfold naturally," he admitted. What he could control, though, he controlled.
"What I tried to do is look at what the players needed. If there's a longer game, they needed some energy or something to eat, so I made sure they had it available instead of spending time getting it themselves around the third or fourth hour."
Viewers watching the live broadcast of the games got to witness the results of that instinct in real time, with water bottles, bananas, and coffee cups appearing at just the right moments.
Build-up: Virtual camps, and logistics that nearly derailed things again
The challenges for Swayams started even before the tournament. Getting the team to that stage was a project in itself, with busy, overlapping schedules making it difficult for the players to train together in person.
With the help of the All India Chess Federation (AICF), the team turned to virtual camps in the run-up to the Olympiad.
"It all started with the camps, like organising the camp online, where we found that most of the players' schedules were very tight, so we held an online camp because players were not able to find a common timing to able to meet up with their busy schedules," Mishra revealed.
The challenges followed the team in Samarkand, where India, like several other nations, faced accommodation and food issues.
"On the first day, with the issues with the stay, AICF stepped up, and the president Nitin Narang and the HOD Abhijit Kunte ensured that the players got the rooms first," he said. "President Narang was also present, and he went out of his way to help us in most of the things."
Food then became another issue, with Mishra recalling that “when food was not very ideal, the options were not great, AICF made sure that food is Indian food people get so that they don't lack energy and they don't go like let's say their routine and other things are not disturbed as well.”
The Vaishali decision
The team bronze did not come easy, without its share of difficult calls. One of the toughest was deciding which four players from the five-member squad would take the board each round.
"For me, it was not easy choosing whom to play, because it was always a tricky call, with Savitha and Vantika performing very well on the last boards, and Vaishali also having good chances; we wanted her to play. It's a very hard call when one of your top players ends up not being in form, and the others are performing very well. Vaishali tried, gave her best, but it just wasn't meant to be," the captain, who then decided to keep the Women's World Championship challenger on the board for only six out of the eleven games, sighed.
With Vaishali, who had just one win in the entire Olympiad and finished with a score of 2.5/6, due to challenge for the Women's World Championship title next year, Mishra also addressed whether this stretch of poor form carried any psychological weight into that bigger picture.
"We had a discussion, and she was not thinking at all about the World Championship. She wanted to just focus and give her best for India in this Olympiad, but it wasn't working out. I think she's strong enough, a professional player who should be able to get back much stronger and prove herself as a world champion as well. I wish she wins the World Championship."
Board-by-board analysis from the captain
"Humpy on board one, I think, this would be her best Olympiad. India hadn't won a medal on board one for quite some time, and her winning one (a bronze with a score of 7/10), undefeated, against strong opposition, was very good. We were never on the back foot on board one," captain Mishra explained.
Board two, however, told a different story.
"Vaishali started off decently. She had some tough opponents who didn't make mistakes and played precisely against her. Against Poland, that's where things changed — she had a better position, in fact, and wanted to win. There were a couple of chances to simplify into a draw, but she wanted to win, and in that process ended up making mistakes and losing," the coach added.
"Then she had another critical game against Kazakhstan, where she again had chances to equalise but wanted to win it for the team. A draw there would have given us 2-2, because Savitha's board wasn't clear yet. So she tried, and it backfired. You can say she was always there for the team, even if her performance wasn't great."
By contrast, individual silver medalist Divya Deshmukh, scoring 6.5/10, emerged as one of the pillars.
"She took a lot of blacks, seven out of ten games, and was always ready whenever the team needed her. She had a consistent performance and gave us a couple of fast wins that put pressure on the other opponents."
It came after a rough patch as Mishra continued, "She started completely out of form; Cairns Cup wasn't as per expectations, GCL wasn't great. But from there, she came back very strongly and was always reliable. She lost the last round, but she'd done her job by then."
Vantika Agrawal, on board four for most of the tournament before Savitha's emergence, drew measured praise.
"She was consistent. There was one game, against China, that was very close, where she was close to a draw and missed something under pressure. Otherwise, she did her job, whatever was assigned to her, and gave us points on the last board," he added.
And then Savitha. Mishra didn't hold back on addressing the scrutiny that had followed her selection.
"There were a lot of people who questioned her spot, journalists saying there are players higher than her, and so on. But according to the selection, she was qualified, and she'd won the Asian continental a couple of months ago. She'd also played the World Women's Team Championship, so I knew her as a team player always.
"Whenever we gave her the opportunity, she delivered. From round seven onwards, her form dropped slightly compared to the initial rounds as she was making some errors; the quality wasn't quite what she'd have expected. But she always compensated in the last hour, changing the result of the match completely. If India won a medal, we owe it to her."
Bronze, and what the team takes from it
Asked whether anyone inside the camp was satisfied with bronze, Mishra didn't pretend otherwise.
"We are not satisfied. The colour of the medal would have been different, and we would have been much happier. But even in your not-so-good times, if you're able to get a medal, that shows how strong the team is. We expect to come back even stronger next year and win gold.
"I know people might be disappointed; the fans might be disappointed; we're equally disappointed. But everyone tried their best. The margins were very close."
The tournament's bigger lesson, for him, had less to do with India specifically than with the state of women's chess as a whole.
"We did not underestimate anyone, but there were a lot of teams creating upsets. Mongolia, whom we played in round four, and Greece in round three, both ended up causing upsets elsewhere. Against the silver-winning Kazakh team, Mongolia were winning too, before it finished 2-2. In the last few Olympiads it was smooth sailing for the top seeds. 
This year, weaker teams were able to strike. That means chess is growing in general, especially women's chess."
It's a tournament Mishra will remember as much for its margins as its medal, a campaign where India were, by his own description, "always on the wrong side of where we wanted to be", rescued more than once by a teenager fuelled on endless cups of coffee, and still, somehow, bronze rather than nothing at all.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Kumkum, Dhiraj face Japan in recurve mixed team semifinal
