briefs.headline: Irani Cup 2026 | Srinagar cricket ground rewrites history to outpace memories of 1983 India-West India fiasco
briefs.deck: With the J&K Cricket Association (JKCA) limiting the crowd strength to a manageable 5000 in the stadium, those who sit in the stands are monitored to ensure the history is not repeated.
briefs.bodyText:
A roar from the crowd reached a crescendo and waned amidst mighty chinars, encircling the Sher-e-Kashmir Cricket Stadium in Srinagar, on Thursday (October 1, 2026) marked the first-ever Irani Cup 2026 match and created history. Cut to 1983, the same ground and the same month saw 21 men storming the ground during the lunch break and damaging the pitch in a bid to disrupt the India versus West Indies match.
With the J&K Cricket Association (JKCA) limiting the crowd strength to a manageable 5000 in the stadium, those who sit in the stands are monitored to ensure the history is not repeated. The Association also screened beforehand the guests and invitees and issued limited passes to the outside crowds, officials told The Hindu.
As the J&K Team dominated the Rest of India at pace on day one of the five-day match, it has buoyed even the political will of the ruling National Conference (NC). “It is a good sign that Kashmir is hosting the Irani Cup 2026. We are happy to see the first-ever five-day match being played in Kashmir,” said Nasir Aslam Wani, NC leader and adviser to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah.
Back on October 13, 1983, the same party, NC, was ruling J&K when 21 men, with 12 accused identified later, waited in the wings till lunch was declared and stormed into the ground to dig the pitch, “in a bid to internationalise the Kashmir issue”. Those accused included two separatist leaders, Shakeel Bakshi and Shabir Ahmad Shah. However, the court acquitted them in 2011 “for lack of evidence”. Locals supported West India more than the Indian team. It took 22 years of trial to decide the case and acquit the accused later.
However, this time the political atmosphere, even though there are multiple security rings, has taken a complete turn with crowds whistling, clapping, bugling and enjoying the match.
“We intend to invest in cricket infrastructure of Kashmir to host IPL matches in the future too. We are indeed in the process of that. Right now, our focus is upgrading the infrastructure in districts and tehsils. We want to hone the skills of local talent and provide a platform to showcase their skills,” said Mr. Wani.
Pointing out the pacer Aquib Nabi, who debuted in a test match for India last month, Mr. Wani said, “Kashmir has cricketing potential. Mr. Nabi already proved it. These kinds of matches will allow our talent not to establish at the local level but at the country level,” said Mr. Wani.
With this Irani Cup rewriting the history on the ground, BCCI chairman Mithun Manhas is enthusiastic to “to bring more matches to Kashmir”. “A match of this level is happening after almost four decades, so it is a matter of great happiness. Cricket has returned. Efforts from the Board will continue and JKCA will have full support of the BCCI so that they can organize matches on a bigger scale and also bring international games,” said Mr. Manhas.
With uncanny celebrations in the stands, the West Indies’ victory over India by 28 runs in 1983 may have restrained the government’s will to host more such matches in the Valley, but the Irani Cup has already succeeded in writing a new chapter of history on the same ground.

briefs.headline: Second-placed Pranavi's 63 puts India in twin medal hunt, Talwar slips to 7th
briefs.deck: Pranavi's two-round tally of 11-under-par 129 leaves her just two shots behind Tan (63-64), who sits at 13-under.
briefs.bodyText:
The unstoppable Pranavi Urs fired a blistering 7-under 63 in the second round that catapulted her into sole second place, just two shots behind leader Shannon Tan of Singapore, in the women's golf competition at the Asian Games here on Thursday.
Urs started her opening round with back-to-back birdies, sinking four in her first six holes before adding three more in a spectacular stretch from the 13th to the 16th.
What was even better was that there was no bogey in her 63.
Her spectacular charge also transformed the women's team competition, lifting India into the bronze-medal position at seven-under-par 273 as Diksha Dagar (71-73) was T-21st and Aditi Ashok (71-74) was T-25. The two best scores in each round count towards the team medals.
Pranavi's two-round tally of 11-under-par 129 leaves her just two shots behind Tan (63-64), who sits at 13-under.
Pranavi was later asked about cricket's popularity and many cricketers taking to golf and she quipped, "I think Virat should start golf, he would make golf so popular in India."
Meanwhile in the men's section, Saptak Talwar (66-68), who was third after the first round slipped in the second round despite 2-under 68 and is now 6-under and tied 7th. The leader is still Taipei's Wang We Hsuan (65-66) at 9-under but he is tied with China's Ding Wenyi, who two years ago won the Asian Amateur Championships in Japan and soon after that turned pro. Ding (67-64) is also 9-under.
Japanese duo Kazuki Higa (65-67) and former Hero Indian Open champion Keita Nakajima (66-66) are tied third.
Japan (264), China (265) and Korea (266) hold the top three spots in men's team competition with India (273) in fifth place, one behind Chinese Taipei (269) who are fourth.
The showing and the bigger picture is not lost on Pranavi. With the Hero Women's Indian Open only a couple of weeks away, a strong Asian Games showing could provide valuable momentum.
"Always good to be in contention. Unfortunately, there haven't been a lot of times where I've been in contention on Tour. So to kind of get that momentum going towards the Hero Women's Indian Open in a couple weeks is a good sign," said the Hero supported golfer.
With 36 holes still to play, India are suddenly in the thick of the battle for medals, possibly gold in both individual and team, Indian women are five behind new leaders China and four behind second placed Singapore.
Pranavi's round had clean ball-striking, aggressive but controlled approach play and enough magic on the greens to keep the birdies flowing.
She began with a 20-foot birdie putt on the first hole and never looked back.
She said, "The game was pretty solid from tee-to-green. Didn’t really have any bad shots. A very good, solid round, and that was that," said Pranavi, summing up a round that was anything but ordinary.
Her secret was hardly complicated.
“I put myself in good positions off the tee, which gave me good numbers to hit the approach shots. Some of the shots that I got, I was really comfortable with those numbers, and I stuck it in to five feet,” she said. “Just hitting fairways and greens, that’s always been my game plan.”
Pranavi’s game held firm and solid and India were in the hunt as she walked off the course.
The round was even more valuable for India because neither of her teammates could match her scoring spree.
Diksha Dagar slipped to tied 21st at four-over, while Aditi Ashok was tied 25th at five-over. Pranavi's seven-under therefore provided the huge injection the Indian team needed, taking them to seven-under overall and into third place behind China and Singapore.
The individual battle, however, is where the drama is likely to intensify. Pranavi will play in the final group in Friday’s third round, just two shots behind Shannon Tan.
“I’ve been out there in the final group a few times, and I’ve always enjoyed it. I’ve enjoyed the pressure,” said Pranavi.
But Pranavi is refusing to get ahead of herself. “I’m not thinking about anything as of now, I’m just thinking about tomorrow’s round.”
When asked about the popularity of cricket and that many cricketers are playing golf now, she said with a smile, "For a change they should come watch us."
She pointed out that several cricketers have taken up golf.
Among them is former India all-rounder Yuvraj Singh, with whom she has played.
"He's a very good player, hits the ball miles, but it can go on either side," she said.
For Pranavi, the next two rounds are a big test. With Tan in her sights, Pranavi enters the final groups on Friday carrying India’s strongest individual medal challenge — while her performance has simultaneously kept the women’s team firmly in the hunt for an Asian Games podium finish.

briefs.headline: Rohit — letting his bat do the talking
briefs.deck: A year is still a long time in international sport and the opener will be nearly 40 and a half when the World Cup gets going. But he is the latest shining example of age being just a number
briefs.bodyText:
If the West Indian – and Indian – bowling fraternities currently doing battle in the One-Day International series decide to go on strike, they will be greeted with empathy, sympathy and understanding. If one thought Sunday’s first game in Thiruvananthapuram was a tall-scoring affair – 595 runs in 91.4 overs, overall run-rate 6.51 – then how do you even begin to describe the massacre in Guwahati on Wednesday?
How often does a team boast three centurions and get beaten out of sight? If you said never, allow yourself a pat on the back. How often does a team rack up 405 and end by licking its wounds? If you said once before, another pat. Though, it must be said, each of these gentle pats will heap untold misery and psychological pain on the Caribbean bowling group.
The thousands at the ground and millions watching on television must have wondered at the wisdom of Shubman Gill’s decision to stick the visitors in after West Indies rode on sparkling centuries from John Campbell, skipper Shai Hope and the free-flowing Amir Jangoo to amass 405 for seven. Only once before in the history of the game, more than a decade back, has a higher total been scaled down in ODI history. On that instance, South Africa rode on the incandescence of Herschelle Gibbs (175), and key contributions from Graeme Smith (90), Mark Boucher (50) and Johan van der Wath (35 off 18) to overhaul Australia’s 434 for four with one wicket and one delivery to spare. A tantalisingly close contest with the result in doubt till the very final ball.
Asense of the inevitable
But not so in Guwahati. There was a sense of the inevitable when India began their reply. To have to score at more than eight an over from the off was a massive ask, on the face of it. Never mind how flat the track, how small the boundaries and how inexperienced the bowling attack, to reel in 405? Not easy, you’d think. Not by a long way. Well, think again.
Gill, perhaps determined to prove that his call to chase was the right one, no matter the mountain ahead of him, raced away with a Formula One beast, engines screaming, rubber burning. At the other end, his predecessor as India’s captain purred along effortlessly, matching his partner for impact without resorting to the rambunctiousness that the man 12 years his junior was showcasing.
The artificial clouds of uncertainty that had been thrust above Rohit Sharma’s head disappeared in a flurry of boundaries at Lord’s some two and a half months back, when the right-hander produced his 34th ODI hundred. His subliminal 138 wasn’t enough to help India overhaul England’s 387 in the deciding game of the three-match series, but coming as it did just a day and a bit after BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia moved to quell speculations that Lord’s would be his swansong, it was a statement of great intent and import.
Rohit would be less than human if he hadn’t felt the heat going into Lord’s. Not because his bat had gone cold, but because the expectations were extraordinarily unfair and demanding, the scrutiny unforgiving, the dissection brutal if without basis. He knew he still had it; he had worked hard to become the fittest version of himself (possibly ever) and it must have rankled that, for all his staggering accomplishments, he was still being put on trial.
Not used to outlandish statements or prickly gestures, Rohit took everything in his stride, silencing wagging tongues and the motley band of critics with the Lord’s masterpiece. Only he can say if that effort freed him up mentally, but on Wednesday, Rohit was at it again, content to sail in Gill’s wake, happy to keep up his end of the bargain and using all his experience, wisdom and intelligence to not try to compete with the fireworks emanating from the other end.
One of the great virtues of having played internationally for 19 years and represented the country in more than 500 matches is that you know your game inside out. You quickly sum up the conditions, you figure out rapidly what works and what may not. You decide which bowlers to target, which areas to score freely in. Having spent 50 overs in the field chasing leather, Rohit knew that to hop on to the backfoot and play from there was a fruitful, productive, paying option. And that’s exactly what he did, hanging just that touch back and letting loose without ever trying to overhit or muscle the ball as he kept his tryst with three-figures.
A spectacle
Gill’s century was a spectacle, spanning just 62 deliveries and containing 10 fours and five sixes. It was as if he was batting on a different, stratospheric plane because that’s how effortlessly easy on the eye he is. But what about Rohit? When has he not been easy on the eye himself? Ever?
Rohit’s hundred came off 72 deliveries – stately it certainly wasn’t. Of those 72 balls, 10 disappeared to the boundary, six over it. On its own, it was a compelling effort, a glorious compilation of some of the prettiest shots you will see on the cricket ground. Gill’s luminescence eclipsed it a little, but only a little. When you set out in quest of 405, individual brilliance won’t cut it. If India managed in the end to scale it down with a massive 39 balls to spare -- and with eight wickets in hand – put it down almost entirely to the opening salvo.
By the time Rohit fell leg before to Jayden Seales, he had breezed to 101, off 75 balls. More importantly, he had helped Gill put on 255, in just 158 deliveries. India were scoring at nearly 10 an over – pause, reflect and marvel – when the Mumbaikar exited the middle of the ACA Stadium off to rapturous applause. Nary an emotion, just another evening in the office, and not a feeling of a job half-done because Rohit knew what incoming No. 3 Virat Kohli was capable of, what the depth in the batting order could translate to, and what was going through his successor’s mind – stay till the finish, get the job done.
Rohit’s celebratory jig during the single that took him from 99 to 100 has been much discussed in the last several hours. When he was asked about that not long after the winning run was struck, he refused to rise to the bait, saying, “I’ll keep that celebration for myself. Some things are just meant to be with you and it’s not to be shared. So that was for me.” And why not? Why, when he had chosen silence to stave off sniping teeth and malicious gossip, did he owe anyone any explanation about his celebration? Why indeed?
Like Kohli had at the start of the series, Rohit also went public before the second ODI about his ambitions, about his quest for the elusive 50-over World Cup winner’s medal. The former boasts one of those, having played a significant role when Mahendra Singh Dhoni’s men created history a decade and a half back by becoming the first host nation to go all the way. Kohli had smashed a century on his World Cup debut in Mirpur against Bangladesh and weighed in with a crucial hand in the final in Mumbai against Sri Lanka. Walking in at a wobbly 31 for the loss of Virender Sehwag and Sachin Tendulkar as India chased 275 for the title and history, he helped current coach Gautam Gambhir put on 83 for the third wicket before perishing for 35.
Kohli was also the Player of the Final when Rohit hoisted the T20 World Cup trophy in Bridgetown two and a quarter years back, so he has the full set of white-ball winners’ medals, so to say. Rohit holds two T20 World Cup champion medals – on debut in 2007 and on his swansong in 2024 – but having heartbreakingly missed out on selection in 2011, slammed five centuries in 2019 and stumbled at the final hurdle, as skipper, in 2023, he is determined, if not desperate, to make his final chance a telling, successful one.
A year is still a long time in international sport and Rohit will be nearly 40 and a half when the World Cup gets going. But he is the latest shining example of age being just a number. Driven by a raging inner fire and happily immune to the goings-on around him, his goal is palpable, his focus narrow, his vision understandably blinkered. In New Zealand in November, when the final preparatory exercise will get underway, he will get five opportunities to refamiliarise himself with the conditions that can be expected to be on offer in Africa.
By his own admission, because he only plays one format internationally, he has the time to revisit his game and deep-dive into analysis, something that constant travel and the hectic hustle and bustle of non-stop cricket can sometimes preclude. Headspace has never been a problem with Rohit. He might have spent much of his career in Kohli’s shadow and was eclipsed by Gill on Wednesday, but Rohit isn’t the sort to dwell on these little things. He has the remarkable ability to always keep the larger picture in mind which, coupled with his experience, his nous and his hunger, make him a cherished teammate and a doubly dangerous opponent.

briefs.headline: Have no issues in my body, feeling good again: Angkrish Raghuvanshi
briefs.bodyText:
Angkrish Raghuvanshi is back where he belongs. He is doing what he loves the most – playing cricket. The 22-year-old was deprived of that blissful feeling after being sidelined for three months with a finger injury, sustained while on Kolkata Knight Riders duty in the IPL.
But Raghuvanshi is on a comeback trail and the runs are starting to flow from his willow. After hitting three half-centuries for Mumbai in the Thimmappaiah Memorial tournament in Karnataka, he struck 51 for Rest of India u-23 on the opening day of the encounter against Tamil Nadu u-23 at the M.A. Chidambaram Stadium on Thursday.
“It was a pretty bad injury, and it took me months to return to cricket. But as a cricketer, you just want to be on the field and play. This is what I want to do. I always want to be on the ground rather than on a hospital bed,” said Raghuvanshi.
“[During my recovery], I had the hunger to get back on the field. Every day I was thinking about how I could get better. The months did not fly... I was like: ‘I should be on the pitch’. I am grateful to be playing cricket again. I have no issues in my body, and I am feeling really good about my batting. I am excited for the season, but I am not looking too far ahead,” he added.
Pillar of strength
An interaction with Raghuvanshi may be incomplete without the mention of Abhishek Nayar, his long-time mentor and head coach at KKR in IPL 2026. “He is everything to me. I have learnt a lot about life and cricket from him. Anytime I have a problem, I go to him. He is a pillar [of support] in my life. I speak to him almost every day”.

briefs.headline: Brazil football team arrives in Kolkata
briefs.bodyText:
Members of the Brazil football team touched down at the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport here on Thursday in a chartered flight for the friendly against India.
For a city that shares a deep-rooted love for football, the arrival of one of world football’s giants was a moment to cherish. Millions of football aficionados in Bengal finally got the chance to welcome their favourite international side.
The arrival also set the stage for the FIFA international friendly, where the Indian men’s national team will take on the might of the Selecao, at the Salt Lake Stadium on Saturday. The creativity, flair and skill of Brazil’s ‘Jogo Bonito’ have long made the Selecao an enduring icon among football-lovers in Bengal and across India. Their presence in Kolkata adds a special emotional dimension to the eagerly-awaited fixture.
The biggest attraction among the visitors is Vinicius Junior. The Real Madrid forward has emerged as one of the leading stars of the modern game, renowned for his pace and dribbling ability.
Vinicius missed the chance to visit India when he was ruled out of the 2017 FIFA U-17 World Cup, hosted by India. Flamengo held him back after their Copa do Brasil final defeat, despite the then 17-year-old having already secured a €45 million move to Real Madrid.
It is a full-circle moment for Vinicius, who has finally arrived in India and again finds himself to be the biggest attraction as Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil prepares to face the Blue Tigers. With Raphinha withdrawing due to injury, the Vinicius factor is only expected to heighten the excitement and galvanise support in Kolkata.

briefs.headline: ‘Where is the contest between bat and ball?’ 811-run ODI raises questions
briefs.deck: India captain Shubman Gill’s unbeaten 223 was sublime, his impeccable timing, placement and voracious appetite hallmarks of his talent. So too was Rohit Sharma’s easy-on-the-eye 101. The West Indies also had three centurions. These batters needed adversaries, and they found none. Not from the bowlers nor from the pitch.
briefs.bodyText:
KOCHI: 811 runs were scored in 93.3 overs in the second ODI between India and West Indies at Guwahati on a ridiculous day of batting, when bowlers were reduced to mute spectators. Once, a match like this would have been celebrated like a historic event. Now, it’s just another game of cricket. A game like this doesn’t thrill the audience; it leaves them weary of watching another run-fest on a pitch described as a ‘national highway’ by Ravi Shastri on commentary.
India captain Shubman Gill’s unbeaten 223 was sublime, his impeccable timing, placement and voracious appetite hallmarks of his talent. So too was Rohit Sharma’s easy-on-the-eye 101. The West Indies also had three centurions. These batters needed adversaries, and they found none. Not from the bowlers nor from the pitch.
“Extremely boring game yaar,” Madan Lal, former medium-pacer and member of India’s 1983 World Cup-winning squad, told TOI.
“Over 800 runs scored on a paata wicket and there was absolutely nothing in it for the bowlers. Give the bowlers something to play with. Where is the contest between bat and ball?" Lal observed.
He reckons that an ideal ODI should end around 280 per side. The kind of game that offers a genuine contest and the one that spectators want to watch. 
For that to happen, he says the curators must put some life into these insipid wickets. “I don’t think that will happen,” he laments.
Former Delhi pacer Sanjiv Sharma attributes the trend to the proliferation of T20Is and expects more teams to chase down 400+ scores in ODIs going forward.
“In T20Is, we see teams chase down 200+ scores. Batters are carrying that confidence into the 50-over format,” he said.
Lal points out that the real worry about such run-fests is that in the long term it kills the quality of bowling. Sharma concurred. “Apart from Kuldeep (Yadav), neither side had a match-winner with the ball. India had a second-string attack, but what about the West Indies? Their bowling was abysmal,” he added.
One-day cricket is in an existential crisis in a calendar surfeit with T20Is. The lure of the 50-over game is that, unlike the T20Is, it gives time for a contest to build, turn and breathe. Gill’s second double hundred in this format will find its way into the record books, but a record without contest is mere arithmetic.

briefs.headline: 2027 Men's ODI World Cup: India to open campaign vs Australia on October 7, play Pakistan on Oct 10
briefs.deck: India will meet Afghanistan on October 14 at the Centurion (Pretoria now known as Tshwane) followed by a match against co-hosts Zimbabwe at the newly constructed Victoria Falls Stadium on October 24.
briefs.bodyText:
India will open their campaign in the men's ICC World Cup against defending champions Australia at the Newlands Stadium in Cape Town on October 7, the world body announced on Thursday (October 1, 2026).
Shubman Gill's men will meet arch-rivals Pakistan at the Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg on October 10.
India will meet Afghanistan on October 14 at the Centurion (Pretoria now known as Tshwane) followed by a match against co-hosts Zimbabwe at the newly constructed Victoria Falls Stadium on October 24.
On October 17, India will be up against a Qualifier in Bloemfontein.
The two semi-finals will be played at Cape Town and Centurion on November 17 and 18 while the final will be played at the Wanderers on November 21.
